front.text: Play the Philidor line with 3...exd4 and 5...Be7 from the first move.

cards.back:
- 2...d6 Black covers the attacked e5-pawn with their d-pawn. This defense is called the 'Philidor Defense'. The move does not develop a piece and locks in the f8-bishop.
- 3.d4 This is White's strongest move. We open the center, prepare the development of the c1-bishop, and attack Black's e5-pawn.
- 3...exd4 Black's best move. Black has no fully satisfactory way to keep the pawn on e5 and therefore captures our d-pawn.
- 4.Nxd4 An easy move. We recapture the pawn and centralize our knight.
- 4...Nf6 A logical choice and the most popular move. Black develops the kingside and attacks our pawn.
- 5.Nc3 Easy one: we cover the pawn and develop our knight.
- 5...Be7 Black develops the bishop and prepares kingside castling. It is a modest setup, but Black's position is rather solid.
- 6.Bf4 The most aggressive move. We plan to play Qd2 and O-O-O next. With our king safely positioned on the queenside, we may attack the kingside by pushing our pawns.
- 6...O-O Black gets their king to safety.
- 7.Qd2 We continue with our plan: secure our king on the queenside and attack on the other side of the board.
- 7...Nc6 claude: Black develops the knight.
- 8.O-O-O We have completed queenside castling and are ready to attack on the kingside.

front.text: Play the Philidor line with 3...Bg4? from the first move.

cards.back:
- 2...d6 Black covers the attacked e5-pawn with their d-pawn. This defense is called the 'Philidor Defense'. The move does not develop a piece and locks in the f8-bishop.
- 3.d4 This is White's strongest move. We open the center, prepare the development of the c1-bishop, and attack Black's e5-pawn.
- 3...Bg4? Black pins our knight, but this move is a well-known mistake since Morphy's game from 1858!
- 4.dxe5! We usually don't want to trade on e5, but this is an exception. Concrete move sequences always beat general concepts.
- 4...Bxf3 Black gives up the bishop pair and speeds up our development, a welcome sight.
- 5.Qxf3 We keep our pawn structure intact, and place our queen on an active square.
- 5...dxe5 Black has restored material equality but will be in deep trouble after our natural reply.
- 6.Bc4 The ideal type of move. We develop our bishop to a great square and threaten mate!
- 6...Nf6 Black develops a piece and stops the mate threat simultaneously.
- 7.Qb3! This queen move is powerful, attacking both b7 and, even more importantly, the f7-pawn with terrible consequences.

front.text: Play the Petroff line with 3...Bb4 from the first move.

cards.back:
- 2...Nf6 Black goes for the Petroff Defense. Instead of covering their e5-pawn, they allow the capture and prefer starting a direct counterattack against our e-pawn.
- 3.Nc3 We cover our attacked e4-pawn, a simple and good reply to the Petroff.
- 3...Bb4 This is Black's best move if they want to avoid 3...Nc6 for some reason. It gives up the e5-pawn, but Black gets enough activity to regain it quickly.
- 4.Nxe5 We grab the central pawn, thank you very much.
- 4...Bxc3 The immediate capture, the most commonly played move. By playing ...Bb4, Black prepared to capture our knight on c3, followed by ...Nxe4.
- 5.dxc3 We always go for this capture here, as we immediately open our bishop on c1.
- 5...d6! An important move!
- 6.Nd3 This is our standard retreat square in this line.
- 6...Nxe4 Black needs to regain the pawn before we cover it by f2-f3.
- 7.Be2 Ready to castle.
- 7...O-O claude: Black castles.
- 8.O-O The initial opening phase is completed. We have castled and are ready for the next phase of the game.

- 3.Nc3 We cover our attacked e4-pawn, a simple and good reply to the Petroff.
- 3...Bc5? Black sacrifices their e-pawn for insufficient compensation.
- 4.Nxe5 Tasty chess! If you can win Black's e-pawn for no obvious compensation, you should go for it.
- 4...Nc6 This is Black's best try and worth investigating.
- 5.Nxc6 The simplest solution.
- 5...dxc6 The only move. We have reached a position that usually arises via a different move order, the 'Stafford Gambit'.
- 6.h3! The little pawn move is essential. Black's idea was to attack our vulnerable f2-spot with ...Ng4, which is a dangerous knight jump.

- 4.Nxe5! We can take the central pawn, based on the idea 4...Nxe5 5.d4, when the fork on bishop and knight regains the piece.
- 4...Nxe5 Black's best defense.

- 5...Bxd4? A welcome sight! Black surrenders the bishop pair and activates our queen!
- 6.Qxd4 Black has a limited choice now, as we attack the knight.
- 6...Qf6 This move introduces fun complications, and it sets a trap.
- 7.Nb5! A cool move to remember! We attack c7, but at the same time, the knight does now protect our queen. Black has no good reply now.

front.text: Play the Three Knights line with 3...d6 from the first move.

cards.back:
- 3...d6 This move is unnecessarily passive. Black's f8-bishop looks rather sad now, as it can't be developed to an active spot on c5 or b4 anymore.
- 4.d4 Very logical, as we intend to play the d-pawn after 3...Nf6 4.d4, going for the Four Knights Scotch. Now we'll likely get a favorable version of this opening.
- 4...Bg4 Black develops their bishop and pins our knight.
- 5.Bb5! A strong move! We develop and pin Black's knight, which increases the pressure on the e5-pawn. We threaten d4-d5 now, with a deadly pin!
- 5...exd4 Black is scared of d4-d5 and takes our pawn to stop our threat.
- 6.Qxd4 We have pinned the black knight, so taking the pawn with the queen is possible.
- 6...Bxf3 Black usually takes on f3, hoping to gain something by doubling our pawns.
- 7.gxf3 Taking the bishop is strong. We plan to castle queenside, so Be3 and O-O-O is the general idea.

front.text: Play the Three Knights line with 3...Bb4 from the first move.

cards.back:
- 3...Bb4 Black continues their kingside development, a move according to general opening principles. It is still not as good as 3...Nf6: the bishop move has a direct drawback that we can exploit.
- 4.Nd5! You shouldn't move the same piece multiple times in the opening... unless it is strong! We lose time by moving our knight again, but we will gain MORE time by hitting Black's bishop with pawn moves.
- 4...Nf6 Black gets the knight into the game and wants to castle soon, a good move.
- 5.c3 Occupying the center by playing c3 & d4 is an attractive idea − let's go for it!
- 5...Bc5 This is the most important move to examine. It is played the most here.
- 6.b4 We attack the bishop again.
- 6...Bb6 Black keeps the bishop on the most active diagonal.
- 7.d4! An important moment. We ignore the threat to our e-pawn and focus on classic opening goals: we occupy the center and want to develop quickly.

front.text: Play the Four Knights Scotch line with 4...Bb4 from the first move.

cards.back:
- 3...Nf6 Black develops the king's knight, which is the best move.
- 4.d4 immediately opens the center and leads to an open position. Black's best reply is 4...exd4.
- 4...Bb4 A rare and slightly dubious move. We can prove an advantage, but only with one reply!
- 5.Nxe5! The only good move! It is not obvious at first sight why you should capture e5 with the knight and avoid other options.
- 5...Nxe4 Black wants to get the pawn back immediately. It's not a good move, but it requires a precise reply.
- 6.Qg4! The best and most fun move to play! We attack both the knight and the g-pawn and enter wild complications.
- 6...Nxc3 The only move available. The knight was attacked, and retreating or covering it failed due to our queen taking g7.
- 7.Qxg7! Wow, what a mess! The position is very favorable for us.

front.text: Play the Four Knights Scotch line with 4...d6 and 5...Bd7 from the first move.

cards.back:
- 3...Nf6 Black develops the king's knight, which is the best move.
- 4.d4 immediately opens the center and leads to an open position. Black's best reply is 4...exd4.
- 4...d6 A passive and dubious move, but it is important to study, as the position may arise from various move orders.
- 5.Bb5! An important move to remember! We pin Black's knight and thus increase the pressure on the e5-pawn. In addition, we also threaten d4-d5, attacking the unlucky pinned knight!
- 5...Bd7 Black addresses the pin, a logical move.
- 6.Bxc6! This move is surprisingly strong, although we give up the bishop for a knight voluntarily.
- 6...Bxc6 The only good reply. Black sets up a counterattack on our e-pawn.
- 7.Qe2! A strong move! We cover the attacked e-pawn, and Black's e-pawn is now in danger again.

front.text: Play the Four Knights Scotch line with 5...Nxd4? from the first move.

cards.back:
- 3...Nf6 Black develops the king's knight, which is the best move.
- 4.d4 immediately opens the center and leads to an open position. Reaching this type of position is a primary concept of our repertoire.
- 4...exd4 Black's best answer is taking our pawn.
- 5.Nxd4 The obvious move to get our pawn back. Our e-pawn is actively placed in the center, controlling the d5-square, and we can easily develop our minor pieces.
- 5...Nxd4? This move is incredibly popular in amateur games. We are happy about this trade, as it only helps to develop our forces.
- 6.Qxd4 Our queen is now in a commanding central position. Black can't develop their f8-bishop to an active square, as we control all of them.
- 6...d6 Passive, but relatively best. Black accepted that the bishop needed to be developed to the modest e7-square.
- 7.Bf4 I like this aggressive move. We want to castle queenside next, followed by a pawn storm on the kingside. Moves like f3, g4, and h4 come to mind.

front.text: Play the Alapin 2...Nc6 line with 3...cxd4 and 4...e6?! from the first move.

cards.back:
- 2...Nc6 Black develops the knight, a logical move. It follows general opening principles and can't be bad. A closer look reveals that it is objectively fine, but Black needs to know or find the correct path on the next moves, or they will get in trouble.
- 3.d4 That was our plan: build a perfect pawn center. Now we get to the first crucial moment.
- 3...cxd4 A natural move, but we are always happy about this trade, as we are granted the additional option Nc3.
- 4.cxd4 And we have reached the second critical position of this line.
- 4...e6?! If they don't play 4...d5, they are in trouble.
- 5.d5! We gain more space with a tempo gain.
- 5...exd5 Black usually takes on d5.
- 6.exd5 claude: We take back and keep a pawn on d5.
- 6...Ne5 Not 6...Nce7?? 7.d6 Ng6 8.Qe2+, winning a piece.
- 7.Nf3 This simple move speeds up our development. We have some advantage. The pawn on d5 gives us more space, and we are the first to castle and use the e-file.

front.text: Play the Alapin 2...e6 line with 3...cxd4?! from the first move.

cards.back:
- 2...e6 Black prepares the move ...d5, an idea similar to the French Defense.
- 3.d4 The automatic reply, completing our central pawn duo.

- 4.cxd4 As always, we are happy about this trade. We'll gain the c3-square for our knight.
- 4...d5 This is best. Black needs a pawn on a central square, attacking our e-pawn.
- 5.e5! I suggest advancing the pawn. Without the c-pawns, we can develop our queen's knight to its most active square on c3.
- 5...Nc6 The most popular and best move. Black wants to put pressure on our d-pawn.
- 6.Nf3 The best square for our knight. We cover d4 and prepare kingside castling.

- 4.exd5 This move aligns with our repertoire choice against the French Defense.
- 4...exd5 Black takes with the pawn and avoids the transposition after the queen move.
- 5.Bb5+ We want to develop quickly: our knight to f3 and our bishop to b5, trying to castle as fast as possible.

cards.back:

- 3.exd5 Taking the pawn is best. We open the position and have good chances to gain a bit of time on Black's queen after their recapture.
- 3...Qxd5 As long as our pawn is on c3, the queen can't be attacked by the move Nc3.
- 4.d4 Our natural reply. Now we need to consider three basic scenarios.

- 5.cxd4 Now we are ready to play Nc3, developing with tempo.
- 5...Nc6 Black attacks our d-pawn, a very logical and popular move.
- 6.Nf3 We need to cover our pawn.
- 6...Bg4 The most active and most popular move for Black.
- 7.Be2 We need to break the pin first.

- 8.Bxf3 Of course, we played Be2 to enable this move.
- 8...Qxd4?? Black had to retreat the queen.
- 9.Bxc6+ We take the queen's sole defender with check and win on the spot.
- 9...bxc6 claude: Black takes back.
- 10.Qxd4 This sequence has happened in tens of thousands of games!

cards.back:

front.text: Play the Alapin 2...Nf6 line with 5...Nc6 from the first move.

cards.back:
- 2...Nf6 Black attacks our e-pawn with their knight, forcing the pawn forward.
- 3.e5 It makes no sense to protect the e-pawn with a passive move − advancing it with a gain of time is much better.
- 3...Nd5 Black occupies this nice central post with their knight.
- 4.d4 As we usually start with the pawn move in other lines of the Alapin, I suggest sticking to this approach here as well.
- 4...cxd4 An almost automatic reply.
- 5.Nf3 Developing our knight first gives us some additional options. Black can't prevent cxd4 anyway.
- 5...Nc6 Developing the knight is a very natural and logical move. Black opts for this most of the time.
- 6.cxd4 I suggest this simple capture to restore material equality.
- 6...d6 Attacking our e-pawn makes a lot of sense, but Black delays kingside development for a while.
- 7.Bc4 Our natural bishop post in this chapter. We get one move closer to kingside castling and attack Black's knight in the process.

front.text: Play the Alapin 2...Nf6 line with 5...e6 from the first move.

cards.back:
- 2...Nf6 Black attacks our e-pawn with their knight, forcing the pawn forward.
- 3.e5 It makes no sense to protect the e-pawn with a passive move − advancing it with a gain of time is much better.
- 3...Nd5 Black occupies this nice central post with their knight.
- 4.d4 As we usually start with the pawn move in other lines of the Alapin, I suggest sticking to this approach here as well.
- 4...cxd4 An almost automatic reply.
- 5.Nf3 Developing our knight first gives us some additional options. Black can't prevent cxd4 anyway.
- 5...e6 A sensible move, as Black wants to get closer to kingside castling.
- 6.cxd4 In all cases, we regain the pawn with cxd4 and develop our bishop to c4.
- 6...d6 This is Black's most popular choice, attacking the e5-pawn.
- 7.Bc4 The best development option for our bishop.

cards.note: What are the first 2 moves of Philidor's Defense?

front.text: Why does the Philidor Defense have the reputation of being slightly passive?

cards.back:
2...d6 covers the e5-pawn but does not develop a piece and locks in the f8-bishop. Compared to Black's main options, [2...Nc6] or [2...Nf6], the king's bishop can't join the game early on, for example on the squares c5 or b4. Black voluntarily limits their options.

The defense is named after François-André Danican Philidor, the strongest player of the 18th century, who coined the quote 'Pawns are the soul of Chess'.

cards.note: What is your third move against Philidor's Defense?

front.text: Besides attacking the e5-pawn, what does 3.d4 do?

cards.back:
This is White's strongest move. We open the center and prepare the development of the c1-bishop.

[3.Nc3] and [3.Bc4] are good moves that follow basic principles (development), but the immediate 3.d4 exerts more pressure, often leading to an inferior reply.

cards.note: Which 3 Black responses to 3. d4 are most common?

front.text: What is your move after 3...Nc6 and why? What other moves are good?

cards.back:
4.Nc3 leads to a position that we investigate via 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 d6 4.d4, with a nice advantage.

White has some other good options, like the logical moves [4.Bc4] or [4.Bb5], but playing 4.Nc3 fits best to our concept. 3...Nc6 is much better than 3...Bg4?, but it gives us a wide range of good moves.

front.text: After 3...Nc6, why don't we take on e5?

cards.back:
[4.dxe5 dxe5 5.Qxd8+ Kxd8] is not as promising as it looks at first sight. Black has lost castling rights, but this is less of an issue after queens were traded.

In general, I advise against trading on e5 in this central configuration (e4&d4 vs. e5&d6), as we trade a more active pawn for a passive one and therefore help Black to gain scope for their pieces, in particular the king's bishop, which is limited by the d6-pawn.

front.text: How do we meet Black's rare third moves, anything other than 3...exd4, 3...Bg4 and 3...Nc6?

cards.back: Other moves are rare and best met with healthy development: we play our knight to c3, develop the bishop to c4 and castle kingside next.

front.text: What is your move after 3...exd4 and why?

cards.back:
4.Nxd4 An easy move. We recapture the pawn and centralize our knight. A key idea of playing an early d4 is removing the e5-pawn to gain control of this central square for our knight.

3...exd4 is Black's best move. Black has no fully satisfactory way to keep the pawn on e5 and therefore captures our d-pawn.

front.text: What are Black's 2 main moves after 4.Nxd4 ?

cards.back:
- [4...Nf6] is a logical choice and the most popular move. Black develops the kingside and attacks our pawn.
- [4...c5]? is dubious. It leads to a structure that we examine via [4...Nf6 5.Nc3 c5], a similar idea.

front.text: What is your move after 4...c5? and why?

cards.back:
5.Ne2 It looks odd, but it follows the same concept as [4...Nf6 5.Nc3 c5 6.Nde2].

claude: Black has weakened the d5-square, and from e2 the knight can reach it via f4.

front.text: What is your move after 4...Nf6 and why?

cards.back: 5.Nc3 Easy one: we cover the pawn and develop our knight.

front.text: What are Black's 5 main moves after 5.Nc3 ?

cards.back:
- [5...Be7] is Black's best move. Black develops the bishop and prepares kingside castling. It is a modest setup, but Black's position is rather solid.
- [5...c5]? is a mistake, a short-sighted attack on our knight.
- [5...g6], [5...c6] or [5...Nc6] are rare alternatives. Against all these setups, we can play as we do against 5...Be7, by developing our bishop to f4, followed by Qd2 and O-O-O.

front.text: What are the next 9 plies following 5...Be7, and what is the plan behind them?

cards.back:
- 6.Bf4 The most aggressive move. We plan to play Qd2 and O-O-O next. With our king safely positioned on the queenside, we may attack the kingside by pushing our pawns (f3&g4 comes to mind).
- 6...O-O Black gets their king to safety.
- 7.Qd2 We continue with our plan: secure our king on the queenside and attack on the other side of the board.
- 7...Nc6 claude: Black develops the knight.
- 8.O-O-O We have completed queenside castling and are ready to attack on the kingside.
- 8...Nxd4 claude: Black trades knights.
- 9.Qxd4 claude: we recapture with the queen.
- 9...Re8 claude: Black brings the rook to the e-file.
- 10.f3 followed by g4 and h4, the pawn storm on the kingside. It is difficult for Black to generate any counterplay.

White has some good alternatives, in particular [6.g3], intending Bg2 and O-O. Both sides' forces are not in direct contact, which gives us a range of options.

front.text: What are the two drawbacks of 5...c5? ?

cards.back:
Black attacks our strong knight, but the cure is worse than the disease. Every pawn move involves a commitment and may weaken crucial squares or pawns.

- The d6-pawn can't be protected by a fellow pawn anymore, and it is a 'backward pawn' on a half-open file. We have good chances to put pressure on the pawn − ideas like a later Bf4 and rooks to the d-file come to mind.
- Even more serious: Black has left the d5-square, a key central point, open for our pieces to use. Black can't control this square with a pawn anymore, and we have excellent chances to establish a strong piece on this outpost square.

front.text: After 5...c5? our knight is attacked. Where does it go and why? Which knight move is less precise?

cards.back:
6.Nde2 We block our own bishop's development, but there is a major upside. Black has weakened the d5-square, which would be ideal for a knight. Our c3-knight is already connected to the square, and from e2 our second knight can quickly reach d5 via the f4-square.

[6.Nb3] is less precise: rerouting the knight to d5 is much more difficult. You could go via b3-d2-c4-e3, which takes ages.

White has a strong alternative in [6.Bb5+], but I prefer the knight maneuver (Nd4-e2-f4) because of its instructional value.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 6...Be7?

cards.back:
- 7.Nf4 claude: the knight heads for d5.
- 7...O-O claude: Black castles.
- 8.Bc4 This demonstrates our basic idea. We have full control of d5 and Black suffers due to a bad e7-bishop and a potentially weak d-pawn.

cards.note: What is your move after 3...Bg4? and why? Black's 2 common responses

front.text: What are Black's 4 main moves after 4.dxe5! and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [4...Bxf3] Black gives up the bishop pair and speeds up our development, a welcome sight.
- [4...dxe5]? [4...dxe5 | 5.Qxd8+ Kxd8 6.Nxe5] is fantastic for White. We win the most important pawn on the board, spoil Black's castling rights, and even win time by attacking Black's g4-bishop.
- [4...Nc6] or [4...Nd7]: in both cases, we can take on d6 and enjoy an extra pawn.

cards.note: What are the next 3 plies following 4...dxe5? ?

front.text: What is your move after 4...Nc6 and why?

cards.back: 5.exd6 We can take on d6 and enjoy an extra pawn.

front.text: What is your move after 4...Nd7 and why?

cards.back: 5.exd6 As after [4...Nc6], we can take on d6 and enjoy an extra pawn.

front.text: Why do we recapture on f3 with the queen?

cards.back: We keep our pawn structure intact, and place our queen on an active square. After Black's logical reply, the queen's position will be put to good use: [5...dxe5 6.Bc4] threatens mate.

cards.note: What are Black's 2 most common responses to the checkmate threat 6.Bc4 ?
After 6...Qf6 what are the next 3 plies and what shouldn't White do?
After 6...Nf6 what are the next 3 plies?

front.text: After 7.Qb3!, Black defends the b-pawn with 7...b6?? . What are the next 3 plies?

cards.back:
Black can't give up the f-pawn.

- 8.Bxf7+ claude: the f-pawn falls with check.
- 8...Kd7 claude: the king has to step out.
- 9.Qe6# checkmate.

front.text: After 7...Qe7, White has two excellent choices. Which are they, and what does each go for?

cards.back:
7...Qe7 is the relatively best solution, as played in the famous Opera Game.

- [8.Qxb7] wins a clean pawn and secures a large advantage.
- [8.Nc3] is Morphy's move, playing for an attack!

front.text: What are the first 2 moves of Petroff's Defense?

cards.back: 2...Nf6 Black goes for the Petroff Defense. Instead of covering their e5-pawn, they allow the capture and prefer starting a direct counterattack against our e-pawn.

front.text: What is the Petroff's reputation, and why is it not played that often in amateur games?

cards.back: The Petroff has a good reputation on the professional level, but is not played that often in amateur games. One reason is that some of the resulting positions are often labeled as 'boring', but this largely depends on the player's ambitions.

front.text: What is your third move against the Petroff and why? Which 2 other moves does White have?

cards.back:
3.Nc3 We cover our attacked e4-pawn, a simple and good reply to the Petroff.

This move makes a lot of sense in the context of our repertoire, as [2...Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4] is a cornerstone of our concept. By answering the Petroff with 3.Nc3, we invite a transposition to this line.

White has a fundamental choice between [3.Nxe5], [3.d4], and the move I suggest, 3.Nc3.

front.text: What are Black's 4 main moves after 3.Nc3, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [3...Nc6 4.d4] leads to the starting position of the Four Knights Scotch and looks like Black's best and most reliable option, but they often play differently.
- [3...Bb4] is the best alternative, but gives White a small advantage.
- [3...Bc5]? is an incorrect gambit.
- [3...d6] is possible, but not in the spirit of the Petroff. After [3...d6 | 4.d4], we'll reach positions that usually occur via the Philidor Defense move order.

front.text: What is your move after 3...Nc6, and where does it lead?

cards.back: 4.d4 We reach the starting position of the Four Knights Scotch, as after [2...Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4]. 3...Nc6 looks like Black's best bet.

front.text: What is your move after 3...d6, and where does it lead?

cards.back:
4.d4 We'll reach positions that usually occur via the Philidor Defense move order [2...d6 3.d4 Nf6 4.Nc3], when [4...exd4 5.Nxd4] would transpose to our chapter on the Philidor.

3...d6 is possible, but not in the spirit of the Petroff.

front.text: What is your move after 3...Bb4 and why? What did Black prepare?

cards.back:
4.Nxe5 We grab the central pawn, thank you very much. Black has not blundered the pawn though. By playing ...Bb4, they prepared to capture our knight on c3, followed by ...Nxe4.

3...Bb4 is Black's best move if they want to avoid 3...Nc6 for some reason. It gives up the e5-pawn, but Black gets enough activity to regain it quickly.

front.text: After 4.Nxe5, Black has various ways to recover the pawn. What are the 3 main points of our concept?

cards.back:
Black may do it in a different order, but in all cases, our concept looks similar:

- They could play ...Qe7 or ...d6 to attack our knight. We should retreat to d3, attacking Black's bishop in the process.
- We want to quickly secure our king by playing Be2 and O-O.
- If Black takes on c3, we always recapture with the d-pawn. This helps to speed up our development, as the c1-bishop gains immediate scope.

front.text: What are Black's 4 main moves after 4.Nxe5, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [4...Bxc3] The immediate capture is the most commonly played move.
- [4...d6 5.Nd3 Bxc3 6.dxc3 Nxe4 7.Be2], with O-O next.
- [4...Qe7 5.Nd3 Bxc3 6.dxc3 Nxe4 7.Be2] is a similar story.
- [4...O-O 5.Nd3 Bxc3 6.dxc3 Nxe4 7.Be2] leads to the same scenario.

These positions are a bit more comfortable for White. We'll see the same structure in our main line.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 4...d6 ?

cards.back:
- 5.Nd3 We retreat to d3, attacking Black's bishop in the process.
- 5...Bxc3 claude: Black takes, to get at our e-pawn.
- 6.dxc3 If Black takes on c3, we always recapture with the d-pawn.

After [6...Nxe4 7.Be2] we castle next.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 4...Qe7 ?

cards.back:
- 5.Nd3 We retreat to d3, attacking Black's bishop in the process.
- 5...Bxc3 claude: Black takes, to get at our e-pawn.
- 6.dxc3 We always recapture with the d-pawn.

[6...Nxe4 7.Be2] is a similar story as after 4...d6.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 4...O-O, and which other fifth move works?

cards.back:
- 5.Nd3 (or [5.Be2])
- 5...Bxc3 claude: Black takes, to get at our e-pawn.
- 6.dxc3 We always recapture with the d-pawn.

[6...Nxe4 7.Be2] leads to the same scenario.

front.text: What is your move after 4...Bxc3 and why?

cards.back: 5.dxc3 We always go for this capture here, as we immediately open our bishop on c1.

front.text: What are Black's 2 main moves after 5.dxc3, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [5...d6]! An important move!
- [5...Nxe4]?? Black must avoid this: [5...Nxe4 | 6.Qg4]! is a good line to know!

front.text: What do you play after 5...Nxe4?? and why?

cards.back: 6.Qg4! A good line to know! We attack not only the knight but also the g-pawn! Black has no good defense against this double attack!

front.text: What are the next 5 plies following 5...d6!, and why not back to f3?

cards.back:
- 6.Nd3 This is our standard retreat square in this line.
- 6...Nxe4 Black needs to regain the pawn before we cover it by f2-f3.
- 7.Be2 Ready to castle.
- 7...O-O claude: Black castles.
- 8.O-O The initial opening phase is completed. We have castled and are ready for the next phase of the game.

It's not a clear mistake to move the knight to f3 ([6.Nf3]), but going to d3 has two advantages.

- From d3, our knight can jump to f4 later, aiming at d5. This is a more effective spot than on f3.
- At a later stage, we can play f2-f3 to push back Black's centralized knight.

front.text: What are Black's 2 main moves after 8.O-O, and which idea of ours does each show?

cards.back:
- [8...Nc6 9.f3 Nf6 10.Bg5] illustrates the idea to evict Black's e4-knight.
- [8...d5 9.Nf4 c6 10.Be3 Nd7 11.c4] shows how Nf4 can help us to open the position for our bishops.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 8...Nc6, and why is the last one unpleasant?

cards.back:
- 9.f3 The already mentioned idea to evict Black's e4-knight.
- 9...Nf6 claude: The knight has to go back.
- 10.Bg5 is very unpleasant for Black, as there is no simple way to break the pin.

front.text: What are the next 5 plies following 8...d5 ?

cards.back:
- 9.Nf4 claude: The knight jumps to f4, as planned, and attacks d5.
- 9...c6 claude: Black covers the pawn.
- 10.Be3 claude: We develop the bishop.
- 10...Nd7 claude: Black develops the knight.
- 11.c4 shows how Nf4 can help us to open the position for our bishops.

front.text: What is the conclusion on the Petroff with 3.Nc3 ?

cards.back:
We answer the Petroff with 3.Nc3, when Black's best option is 3...Nc6, transposing to the Four Knights.

The gambit move 3...Bc5? is incorrect, while 3...Bb4 is solid, but comfortable for White. We usually get the pair of bishops in an open position, which is a good opening result.

front.text: What is your move after 3...Bc5? and why?

cards.back:
4.Nxe5 Tasty chess! If you can win Black's e-pawn for no obvious compensation, you should go for it.

With 3...Bc5? Black sacrifices their e-pawn for insufficient compensation.

front.text: What are Black's 2 main moves after 4.Nxe5, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [4...Nc6] is Black's best try and worth investigating.
- [4...d6] You sometimes see this, but after [4...d6 | 5.Nf3] Black has no compensation for the pawn at all.

front.text: What is your move after 4...d6, and how do you continue?

cards.back: 5.Nf3 Black has no compensation for the pawn at all. We are ready for Be2 and O-O, and may play d2-d4 soon to occupy the center.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 4...Nc6, and which other fifth move is not bad either?

cards.back:
- 5.Nxc6 The simplest solution. The alternative [5.Nf3] is not bad either.
- 5...dxc6 claude: Black takes back with the d-pawn.
- 6.h3! A somewhat unusual, but strong move. It is uncommon and usually wrong to move a flank pawn early in the game, as we have more pressing things to do − develop pieces, occupy the center, etc. Here, however, the little pawn move is essential. Black's idea was to attack our vulnerable f2-spot with ...Ng4, which is a dangerous knight jump.

front.text: After 5.Nxc6, why must Black take back with the d-pawn?

cards.back: [5...dxc6] is the only move, as [5...bxc6]? [5...bxc6 | 6.d4] looks terrible.

front.text: After 5...dxc6, which gambit have we reached, and by which move order does it usually arise?

cards.back:
The 'Stafford Gambit'. It arises after [3.Nxe5 Nc6]?, when [3.Nxe5 Nc6 | 4.Nxc6 dxc6 5.Nc3 Bc5] leads us to the position we currently have on the board.

The Stafford is an incorrect gambit, but it sets some pitfalls for White to navigate. If Black answers our 3.Nc3 with 3...Bc5?, it is likely that they were intending to play the Stafford and now try to transpose to their gambit line. We are happy to oblige, as there is more than one clean refutation.

front.text: After 5...dxc6, why not develop with 6.Bc4 ?

cards.back:
A sample line to illustrate the dangers: [6.Bc4]?? [6.Bc4 | 6...Ng4]! [6.Bc4 Ng4 | 7.O-O Qh4] and White already collapses due to the threats on h2 and f2!

To avoid these kind of disasters, just play 6.h3! and stop Black's key attacking idea.

front.text: What are Black's 2 main moves after 6.h3! and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
Black's game is running out of steam quickly.

- [6...Qd4 7.Qf3] stops the mate and plans d2-d3 and Be3 next.
- [6...O-O 7.d3] covers e4 reliably and intends Be2 and O-O next.

All in all, Black's pawn sacrifice is clearly insufficient. Make sure to remember the move 6.h3!, stopping Black's ...Ng4 attacking plan.

front.text: What is your move after 6...Qd4 and why?

cards.back: 7.Qf3 stops the mate and plans d2-d3 and Be3 next.

front.text: What is your move after 6...O-O, and how do you continue?

cards.back: 7.d3 covers e4 reliably and intends Be2 and O-O next. Once we have played d2-d3, Bc1-e3 is a logical idea to trade off Black's most active piece.

front.text: What are the first moves of the Three Knights Game?

cards.back: 3.Nc3 develops the knight and defends e4. Black's best reply is 3...Nf6, entering the Four Knights Game.

front.text: What is Black's best reply to 3.Nc3, and which logical-looking alternative do we look at here?

cards.back:
- [3...Nf6], entering the Four Knights Game. The most popular choice on all levels; masters play more or less only this, as they know the alternatives are inferior.
- [3...Bc5]?! develops the bishop and increases control over d4, so it looks logical, but it has a severe drawback. Your opponents will often choose it.

front.text: What is your move after 3...Bc5?! and why?

cards.back: 4.Nxe5! We can take the central pawn, based on the idea 4...Nxe5 5.d4, when the pawn forks bishop and knight and regains the piece. Our knight 'sacrifice' is not a real sacrifice but a trade based on a tactic.

front.text: What are Black's 5 main moves after 4.Nxe5! and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [4...Nxe5 5.d4] is the most common. We restore material equality and gain some advantage, but there are a few traps to avoid.
- [4...Bxf2+]?! is dubious but leads to fun complications. Black returns the piece and thus avoids the fork trick.
- [4...Nf6 5.Nxc6 dxc6 6.h3]: White is much better, as Black has no compensation for the pawn.
- [4...Qh4 5.g3] or [4...Qf6 5.Ng4] are easily defused attempts at a Scholar's Mate.

front.text: What do you play after 4...Qh4? and why?

cards.back: 5.g3 An easily defused attempt for a Scholar's Mate. claude: Black threatens ...Qxf2#; the pawn attacks the queen and shuts the h4-e1 diagonal, and we stay a pawn up.

front.text: What do you play after 4...Qf6? and why?

cards.back: 5.Ng4 An easily defused attempt for a Scholar's Mate. claude: Black threatens ...Qxf2#; the knight retreats out of the queen's attack, hits the queen and covers f2, and we stay a pawn up.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 4...Nf6?

cards.back:
- 5.Nxc6 claude: We trade off the attacked knight.
- 5...dxc6 claude: Black recaptures.
- 6.h3 White is much better, as Black has no compensation for the pawn. The same position arises via 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3 Bc5? 4.Nxe5 Nc6 5.Nxc6 dxc6 6.h3.

front.text: What is your move after 4...Nxe5 and why?

cards.back: 5.d4 We regain our piece, forking two minor pieces. 4...Nxe5 is Black's best defense.

front.text: What are Black's 2 main moves after 5.d4, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
Black's path to a reasonable game is narrow.

- [5...Bd6] is Black's best bet and the only way to reach a playable position, but it is still nice for White.
- [5...Bxd4]? You'll meet this a lot, and we'll get a huge advantage.

front.text: What is your move after 5...Bxd4? and why is it a welcome sight?

cards.back: 6.Qxd4 A welcome sight! Black surrenders the bishop pair and activates our queen. Black has a limited choice now, as we attack the knight.

front.text: What are Black's 4 main moves after 6.Qxd4, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [6...Qf6] introduces fun complications.
- [6...Nc6 7.Qxg7] or [6...Ng6 7.Qxg7] is simple: both knight moves are blunders.
- [6...d6] is better, but White is in great shape.

front.text: What do you play after 6...Nc6?? and why?

cards.back:
7.Qxg7 is simple. claude: Once the knight leaves e5, the diagonal to g7 is open; we win a pawn and attack the rook on h8.

The same goes for [6...Ng6 7.Qxg7].

front.text: What is your move after 6...d6, and what is the plan? Why not 7.f4 at once?

cards.back:
7.Be3 or [7.Bd2], and White is in great shape. We prepare queenside castling and are ready to attack the knight on e5 with f2-f4 later.

Not at once: [7.f4 Qh4+]! is annoying because we can't play [7.f4 Qh4+ 8.g3 Nf3+]!

front.text: What is your move after 6...Qf6 and why?

cards.back: 7.Nb5! A cool move to remember! We attack c7, but at the same time, the knight does now protect our queen. Black has no good reply now.

front.text: After 6...Qf6, why not attack the queen with 7.Nd5?

cards.back:
Black's last move set a trap. If we'd attack with 7.Nd5??, they have [7.Nd5 Nf3+]!, winning our queen! claude: the knight check uncovers Black's queen on ours.

This is why 7.Nb5! is so strong.

front.text: What are Black's 2 main moves after 7.Nb5! and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
Black has no good reply now.

- [7...Kd8 8.Qc5]! is powerful.
- [7...c6 8.Nd6+] and Black's position is lost.

front.text: What is your move after 7...Kd8 and why?

cards.back: 8.Qc5! is powerful. We threaten c7, but also Qf8+!

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 7...c6?

cards.back:
- 8.Nd6+ Much simpler than [8.Nc7+ Kd8], when Black can hope for the ...Nf3+ discovery again. We gain some time with the check.
- 8...Kf8 claude: The king steps out of the check.
- 9.Be3 is allowed thanks to that check. Our queen is secured now against the knight discovery, and Black's position is lost. Our d6-knight is dominating, and their king is stranded on f8.

front.text: What is the conclusion on 3...Bc5?! and what must we put up with in the 4...Bxf2+ line?

cards.back:
3...Bc5 follows general opening principles but has a substantial drawback. We have the strong reply 4.Nxe5!, which often leads to favorable complications.

Some positions are excellent for White, but there are some pitfalls we must avoid. The best example is 4...Bxf2+, which is great for White, but our king is vulnerable. We usually want a safe king, but here we must endure this inconvenience because the upsides (center, bishop pair) are enormous.

That 3...Bc5?! 4.Nxe5! is promising for White is a huge incentive to play 3.Nc3, compared to other options. Black will often get into unexpected trouble.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 5...Bd6?

cards.back:
- 6.dxe5 We restore material equality, an easy move.
- 6...Bxe5 claude: Black recaptures.
- 7.Bd3 The final move to remember. We develop our bishop and prepare kingside castling, a similar picture as in the main lines of the Four Knights Scotch, which also features the bishop development to d3.

front.text: After 6...Bxe5, why does the bishop go to d3 and not to c4?

cards.back: It looks more active to place it on c4, but after [7.Bc4 Nf6 8.O-O O-O] Black has secured the f7-spot and puts some pressure on e4 (taking on c3 and ...Nxe4 is an idea).

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 7...Nf6, and how do we stand?

cards.back:
- 8.O-O claude: We castle, as prepared by 7.Bd3.
- 8...O-O claude: Black castles too.
- 9.Bg5 White has a comfortable position. Our pieces are more active than Black's, and we have established an annoying pin. See the game Szwed-Romanishin for more information.

front.text: Black doubles your pawns with 7...Bxc3+. Do you need to worry, and why?

cards.back:
8.bxc3 claude: We recapture.

We don't need to worry about 7...Bxc3+ or similar lines that double our pawns. Black gives up the most powerful piece in return for a weakening of our pawns, which is tough to exploit. Black has no pieces out to attack our queenside pawns while we gain additional possibilities. Later, we might play Ra1-b1-b5 or c3-c4 and Bc1-b2, for example.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 4...Bxf2+?!

cards.back:
- 5.Kxf2 We have to take the bishop, no choice.
- 5...Nxe5 Black restores material equality.
- 6.d4 Completes our dream pawn center and hits Black's knight, winning time.

front.text: After 5.Kxf2, why can't Black give a queen check instead of recapturing with 5...Nxe5?

cards.back:
- [5...Qh4+ 6.g3] claude: the pawn blocks the check and hits the queen.
- [5...Qf6+ 6.Nf3] claude: the knight blocks the check and escapes.

Either way we keep the extra piece.

front.text: After 6.d4, what are White's pluses and problem, and what are Black's 2 most common responses?

cards.back:
We have an excellent pawn center and the pair of bishops, two significant pluses. The problem: our king had to move and looks vulnerable on f2, so we must be careful until it is on a safer spot.

- [6...Qf6+]? is Black's most popular choice, but it is a mistake that only helps us.
- [6...Ng6] is Black's relatively best choice.

front.text: What is your move after 6...Qf6+? and why?

cards.back:
7.Kg1 The safest spot for our king in the long run. 6...Qf6+? is a very tempting move, getting the queen into the game with a check, but it only helps us.

We have established a perfect pawn center and have the pair of bishops, which is a long-term asset, but our king's safety remains a problem. There are various traps that we need to be aware of. If we navigate these traps, our position will be fantastic: we need to solve the short-term problems to preserve our strategic advantages. Don't be afraid of ghosts!

front.text: What knight moves do we look at for Black after 7.Kg1?

cards.back:
- [7...Ne7] sets a trap, but it is not a great move: if we avoid the trap, Black is stuck with their problems.
- [7...Nc6] is met in a similar way.
- [7...Ng4] is the most dangerous trick that Black has. A rare move, but it can be extremely irritating to face.

front.text: What is your move after 7...Ne7 and why? Why not take the knight?

cards.back:
8.Be3 secures the sensitive a7-g1 diagonal. Finally, we threaten to capture the knight.

We are NOT immediately threatening to capture Black's knight after 7.Kg1! [8.dxe5 Qb6+ 9.Be3 Qxe3#] — a disaster!

front.text: After 7...Ne7 8.Be3, what is your plan?

cards.back: Black has to retreat the knight, when we continue with the plan of Qd2, Bc4 and Rf1. You can also consider playing h2-h4 at some point, getting the h1-rook into action this way.

front.text: What is your move after 7...Nc6 and why?

cards.back: 8.Be3 A good reply, similar to the one against 7...Ne7: it secures our strong center.

front.text: After 7...Ng4, what does Black threaten, and why can't you take the knight?

cards.back:
Black threatens ...Qf2#.

It looks like a blunder, but [8.Qxg4 Qxd4+ 9.Be3 Qxe3#] is a familiar pattern by now. We can't take the knight.

front.text: What are the next 7 plies following 7...Ng4, and how do you continue?

cards.back:
- 8.Qd2! The only move that works! There is just one move that covers the mate and keeps the d4-pawn protected. The queen must cover f2, and [8.Qf3 Qxd4+] shows the issue with other squares.
- 8...d6 claude: Black opens the way for the c8-bishop.
- 9.h3 We send Black's knight back home.
- 9...N4h6 claude: The knight has to retreat.
- 10.Nd5 claude: The knight jumps in with an attack on the queen.
- 10...Qd8 claude: The queen retreats.
- 11.Bd3 We have a great position. A way to continue is Qf2, followed by Be3 and Rf1. Black has a misplaced knight on h6, while our knight will find a good route to the kingside via f4.

After 8.Qd2 the queen is on an odd square and our bishop on c1 is unhappy about the situation, but this is a minor problem.

front.text: What are the next 5 plies following 6...Ng6, and which bishop move is less precise?

cards.back:
- 7.Be2 We must get our king to safety and develop the kingside, so we 'castle by hand': we can't play O-O anymore, but Be2, Rf1 and Kg1 reach the same setup. [7.Bc4] has a similar idea.
- 7...d6 claude: Black opens the way for the c8-bishop.
- 8.Rf1 Continuing to castle by hand.
- 8...Nf6 Black develops.
- 9.Kg1 Our 'castling by hand' is complete and the king is safe.

[7.Bd3 Qf6+] is less precise, as our d-pawn is hanging.

front.text: What is your move after 9...O-O? and why?

cards.back: We threaten Bg5 with an annoying pin. After 9...O-O? 10.Bg5, we threaten to destroy Black's kingside by taking on f6, with Nd5 being an additional problem.

front.text: After 9...h6, what is your plan?

cards.back: Black probably needs 9...h6 to stop the pin, but we are in great shape. Bring the queen to the kingside with Qe1-g3, later play Be3, and increase the pressure on the f-file by doubling rooks.

front.text: Besides 3...Nf6 and 3...Bc5, which 2 Black replies to 3.Nc3 do we look at, and how do we feel about them?

cards.back:
[3...d6] and [3...Bb4], Black's third and fourth most popular moves. They are a welcome sight, as we'll get a promising position without any major effort.

3...Bb4 continues Black's kingside development, a move according to general opening principles. It is still not as good as 3...Nf6, the main continuation: the bishop move has a direct drawback that we can exploit.

front.text: What is your move after 3...d6 and why?

cards.back:
4.d4 Very logical, as we intend to play the d-pawn after [3...Nf6 4.d4], going for the Four Knights Scotch. Now we'll likely get a favorable version of this opening, as Black is already committed to a passive setup.

3...d6 is unnecessarily passive. Black's f8-bishop looks rather sad now, as it can't be developed to an active spot on c5 or b4 anymore.

front.text: What are Black's 3 main moves after 4.d4, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [4...exd4 5.Nxd4 Nf6 6.Bb5] is one of the two main continuations.
- [4...Nf6 5.Bb5 exd4 6.Nxd4] is the other. These two sequences lead to the same position, which we examine via the Four Knights Scotch move order, with a nice advantage for White.
- [4...Bg4] Black develops their bishop and pins our knight. This is not the most popular move.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 4...exd4, and where does the line lead?

cards.back:
- 5.Nxd4 claude: We take the pawn back with the knight.
- 5...Nf6 claude: Black develops and attacks e4.
- 6.Bb5 claude: We pin the knight.

This is the position discussed via [3...Nf6 4.d4 d6 5.Bb5 exd4 6.Nxd4], with a nice advantage for White. This pawn structure is also featured in the course's model game.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 4...Nf6, and where does the line lead?

cards.back:
- 5.Bb5 claude: We pin the knight, as in the Four Knights Scotch, where we are now.
- 5...exd4 claude: Black takes the pawn.
- 6.Nxd4 claude: We take it back with the knight.

The same position as after [4...exd4 5.Nxd4 Nf6 6.Bb5], discussed via the Four Knights Scotch, with a nice advantage for White.

front.text: What is your move after 4...Bg4 and why?

cards.back: 5.Bb5! A strong move! We develop and pin Black's knight, which increases the pressure on the e5-pawn. First of all, we threaten d4-d5 now, with a deadly pin!

front.text: After 4...Bg4, why not 5.dxe5 or 5.d5 ?

cards.back:
- [5.dxe5]? It's important to understand that we don't want to trade on e5, as it only helps Black to gain more scope for their pieces. After [5.dxe5 | 5...dxe5], Black would be able to develop the f8-bishop actively. Taking on e5 is not a trade on equal terms, as d4 is a stronger pawn than d6.
- [5.d5] is not bad at all, but closing the center leads to a less dynamic play. 5.Bb5 poses more concrete problems and gives us better chances for a direct attack.

front.text: What are Black's 3 main moves after 5.Bb5! and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [5...exd4] Black is scared of d4-d5 and takes our pawn to stop our threat.
- [5...Bxf3] is no improvement: we can take back with the queen or with the g-pawn.
- [5...a6] is no improvement either: [5...a6 | 6.Bxc6+ bxc6 7.dxe5 Bxf3 8.Qxf3] is great for White.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 5...exd4, and what good alternative do we have on move 7?

cards.back:
- 6.Qxd4 We have pinned the black knight, so taking the pawn with the queen is possible.
- 6...Bxf3 Now Black usually takes on f3, hoping to gain something by doubling our pawns.
- 7.gxf3 Taking the bishop is strong, but inserting [7.Bxc6+ bxc6 8.gxf3] is a good alternative too.

front.text: After 7.gxf3, what is your plan, and where does your king go?

cards.back: We plan to castle queenside, so Be3 and O-O-O is the general idea. Our kingside is no safe place for our king (the doubled f-pawn), which makes the queenside the best spot for the king. The open g-file is often great for a rook, targeting Black's kingside.

front.text: After 5...Bxf3, which 2 recaptures work, and how does each continue?

cards.back:
- [6.Qxf3 exd4 7.Ne2], getting the d-pawn back next.
- [6.gxf3], when [6.gxf3 | 6...exd4 7.Qxd4] transposes to our main line 5...exd4 6.Qxd4 Bxf3 7.gxf3, which is excellent for White.

front.text: After 5...a6, what are the next 3 plies?

cards.back:
- 6.Bxc6+ claude: We take the knight with check.
- 6...bxc6 claude: Black has to recapture.
- 7.dxe5 claude: The e-pawn has lost a defender.

After [7...Bxf3 8.Qxf3] it is great for White. We are much better developed, and Black's queenside pawns are shattered and all weak.

front.text: What is the conclusion on 3...d6 and on 3...Bb4 ?

cards.back:
As usual, an early ...d6 is too passive. After [3...d6 4.d4], we get a comfortable advantage and an easy game.

The move [3...Bb4] follows general opening principles but has a substantial drawback. After the strong [3...Bb4 | 4.Nd5]!, we see a great example of correct tempo play in the opening. Usually, we don't want to move a piece multiple times in the opening. The knight jump is an exception because, in the end, we win MORE time by attacking Black's bishop.

front.text: What is your move after 3...Bb4 and why?

cards.back: 4.Nd5! Well, you shouldn't move the same piece multiple times in the opening... unless it is strong! We lose time by moving our knight again, but we will gain MORE time by hitting Black's bishop with pawn moves such as c3 and even b2-b4 and d2-d4 if they retreat the bishop to c5 or a5.

front.text: What are Black's 3 main moves after 4.Nd5! ?

cards.back:
- [4...Nf6] gets the knight into the game and wants to castle soon, a good move.
- [4...Bc5 5.c3 Nf6 6.b4 Bb6 7.d4] is a likely continuation, leading to the same position as after 4...Nf6 5.c3 Bc5 6.b4 Bb6 7.d4.
- [4...Ba5 5.c3 Nf6 6.b4 Bb6 7.d4]: the same idea also works if Black retreats the bishop to a5, it will lead to the same position.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 4...Bc5, and where does the line lead?

cards.back:
- 5.c3 claude: Prepares b4 and d4.
- 5...Nf6 claude: Black develops.
- 6.b4 claude: We attack the bishop.

After [6...Bb6 7.d4] we have the same position as after 4...Nf6 5.c3 Bc5 6.b4 Bb6 7.d4.

front.text: What is your move after 4...Nf6 and why? What is a good alternative?

cards.back:
5.c3 Occupying the center by playing c3 & d4 is an attractive idea − let's go for it!

A good alternative is [5.Nxb4 Nxb4 6.d4], opening the position differently.

front.text: What are Black's 3 main moves after 5.c3, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [5...Bc5] is the most important move to examine. It is played the most here, and the resulting position after our reply may also occur via the move order 4...Bc5 5.c3 Nf6 6.b4.
- [5...Nxd5]?? is a bad one: we attack two pieces and win one of them!
- [5...Ba5] doesn't lose a piece, but it's still a bad move.

front.text: What do you play after 5...Nxd5?? and why?

cards.back: 6.exd5 We attack two pieces and win one of them! claude: the e-pawn hits the knight on c6 and the c-pawn the bishop on b4.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 5...Ba5, and where does the line lead?

cards.back:
- 6.b4 One good reply of many. 5...Ba5 doesn't lose a piece, but it's still a bad move.
- 6...Bb6 claude: The bishop has to move again.
- 7.d4! claude: The same position as after 5...Bc5 6.b4 Bb6 7.d4.

Now [7...Nxe4 8.Bd3 Nf6 9.Bg5] gives White a strong attack. Black has a hard time dealing with the pinned knight.

front.text: What are the next 11 plies following 5...Bc5, what is a convincing alternative to our first move, and how do we stand?

cards.back:
- 6.b4 We attack the bishop again.
- 6...Bb6 keeps the bishop on the most active diagonal.
- 7.d4! An important moment. Black's knight currently attacks our e-pawn, but there is no simple solution to this attack. The best solution is ignoring the threat to our e-pawn and focusing on classic opening goals. We occupy the center and don't waste time by covering pawns but rather want to develop quickly.
- 7...Nxe4? It's clear that taking e4 is risky for Black.
- 8.Bd3 claude: We develop with an attack on the knight.
- 8...Nf6 claude: The knight goes back.
- 9.Bg5 Black is in trouble. The pin on the knight is tough for Black to handle.
- 9...h6 claude: Black hits the bishop.
- 10.Bxf6 claude: We take the pinned knight.
- 10...gxf6 claude: Forced, as 10...Qxf6 loses the queen to the knight on d5.
- 11.a4 A dream position for White. Black's pawns are a mess, and their king can't safely castle kingside anymore. claude: a4-a5 next threatens to trap the bishop on b6.

6.Bc4 is a convincing alternative, based on [6.Bc4 Nxe4 7.d4 exd4 8.O-O O-O 9.Re1 Nf6 10.Bg5], which gives White a crushing attack. Black's pawn grab 6...Nxe4? is too risky.

front.text: After 6...Bb6, Black's knight attacks e4. Why not trade it off with 7.Nxf6+ or cover the pawn?

cards.back:
We could play [7.Nxf6+ Qxf6], but we'd help Black with their development. Moving our knight again is not ideal. On the other hand, we don't want to cover our e-pawn with a passive move.

The best solution is 7.d4!, ignoring the threat.

front.text: After 7.d4!, what do we threaten and what else must Black worry about?

cards.back: We threaten Bg5 and Black also needs to worry about the e5-pawn. There is no good solution for our opponent, and taking e4 is risky for Black.

front.text: After 7...Nxe4?, why can't you take on e5?

cards.back: We can't play [8.dxe5 Bxf2+]. claude: the pawn has left d4, so the b6-bishop's diagonal to f2 is open and our king is driven out.

cards.note: What is the best move here (a king and bishop position, made in the app; no back)

chapters.name: Four Knights Scotch 4.d4 exd4 − Main Line

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 3...Nf6 ?

cards.back:
- 4.d4 immediately opens the center and leads to an open position. Reaching this type of position is a primary concept of our repertoire.
- 4...exd4 Black's best answer is taking our pawn. The alternatives from the previous chapter are too passive ([4...d6]) or tactically vulnerable ([4...Bb4]).
- 5.Nxd4 The obvious move to get our pawn back.

3...Nf6 develops the king's knight, which is the best move. Now White has some options; I recommend playing 4.d4.

front.text: After 5.Nxd4, what does the central pawn structure give each side?

cards.back:
We have traded our d-pawn for Black's e-pawn. A trade of two central pawns is usually considered a 'fair' deal, as both pawns contribute to controlling the central squares.

- Our e-pawn is actively placed in the center, controlling the d5-square. Due to having moved both our e-pawn and d-pawn, we can easily develop our minor pieces and will castle kingside shortly.
- Black has not yet moved their d-pawn. To complete their development, the d-pawn needs to be involved.

front.text: After 5.Nxd4, which Black move is the only one with good chances to equalize, and why?

cards.back:
[5...Bb4]! Black wants to play their d-pawn to d5, not just to d6, which is too passive. Only by pinning our knight does Black manage to realize this desired central pawn push.

In practice, Black often chooses a different path and suffers.

front.text: What are Black's 5 main moves after 5.Nxd4, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [5...Nxd4]? is very popular below the master level and excellent for White! This premature trade is a large incentive to play the Scotch, as you'll get it so often.
- [5...Bb4]! is best and our chapter's main line.
- [5...Bc5] is Black's second-best move, but we keep an advantage.
- [5...d6]?! can be answered by [5...d6 | 6.Bb5], when we transpose to the previous chapter.
- [5...d5]? is refuted by [5...d5 | 6.Bb5]!, when c6 can't be covered with a good move.

front.text: What do you play after 5...d6?! and where does it lead?

cards.back: 6.Bb5, when we transpose to the previous chapter. [4...d6 5.Bb5 exd4 6.Nxd4] is the alternative move order to reach this position.

front.text: What do you play after 5...d5? and why?

cards.back: 6.Bb5! refutes 5...d5?, as c6 can't be covered with a good move.

front.text: What is your move after 5...Nxd4? and why are we happy to see it?

cards.back:
6.Qxd4 Our queen is now in a commanding central position. Black can't develop their f8-bishop to an active square, as we control all of them.

5...Nxd4? is incredibly popular in amateur games. We are happy about this trade, as it only helps to develop our forces.

front.text: What are Black's 3 main moves after 6.Qxd4, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [6...d6] Passive, but relatively best. Black had no way to develop their bishop actively and accepted that this piece needed to be developed to the modest e7-square.
- [6...b6]? The same problems as after 6...Be7 arise after [6...b6 | 7.e5].
- [6...Be7]? fails because we are threatening e4-e5, pushing Black's knight back.

front.text: What is your move after 6...d6, and what is the plan?

cards.back:
7.Bf4 I like this aggressive move. We want to castle queenside next, followed by a pawn storm on the kingside. Moves like f3, g4, and h4 come to mind, starting our assault on the black kingside. In the meantime, Black has no active counterplay.

This type of position occurs frequently in our repertoire, for example after [4...d6 5.Bb5 exd4 6.Nxd4 Bd7 7.Bxc6 Bxc6 8.Qe2], discussed in the previous chapter; it follows the same mindset.

front.text: After 6...b6?, what are the next 3 plies, and what happens if the knight goes to h5 next?

cards.back:
- 7.e5 The same problems arise as after 6...Be7: we push Black's knight back.
- 7...Bc5 claude: Black develops with an attack on our queen.
- 8.Qf4 claude: The queen steps away and keeps guarding e5.

After [8...Nh5 9.Qf3]! we have a deadly double attack on knight and rook.

front.text: What do you play after 6...Be7? and why?

cards.back: 7.e5 We were threatening e4-e5, pushing Black's knight back. Black needs to return the knight to g8, as [7...Nh5 8.g4] is even worse.

front.text: What three things does 5...Bb4! do for Black?

cards.back:
Black's best move and the only one that leads to a fully satisfactory game for our opponent.

- It addresses Black's need to develop the kingside and castle.
- It fights for the control of d5 by pinning our knight.
- It exerts pressure on our e-pawn.

front.text: What is your move after 5...Bb4! and why?

cards.back: 6.Nxc6 An important move, and the only good one. Black had increased the pressure on our e-pawn, a threat we must address. We must take on c6 first, then develop our bishop.

front.text: After 5...Bb4!, why not cover the e-pawn with 6.f3 or 6.Bd3 ?

cards.back:
- [6.f3]?! is too slow due to [6.f3 | 6...d5]!, when Black manages to open the game after we have lost time and weakened ourselves by playing the f-pawn.
- The best way to cover the e-pawn is developing our bishop to d3, but [6.Bd3]?? [6.Bd3 | 6...Nxd4] is a sad sight.

This leads to the conclusion that we must take on c6 first, then develop our bishop.

front.text: What are Black's 3 main moves after 6.Nxc6, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [6...bxc6] Capturing towards the center is Black's best move.
- [6...Bxc3+]?! surrenders the bishop pair prematurely. After 6...bxc6 7.Bd3, Black will have the same option again.
- [6...dxc6]?! [6...dxc6 | 7.Qxd8+] gives up castling rights for no benefit.

front.text: What is your move after 6...bxc6 and why?

cards.back: 7.Bd3 We develop, protect our pawn and prepare castling − all in one move.

front.text: What are Black's 3 main moves after 7.Bd3, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [7...d5], opening the center, is the most reliable defense for Black.
- [7...O-O 8.O-O] leads to the same defense after 8...d5, or to 8...Re8, a better try for Black than taking on c3.
- [7...Bxc3+]?! [7...Bxc3+ | 8.bxc3] is a questionable trade.

front.text: What are the next 5 plies following 7...d5 ?

cards.back:
- 8.exd5 claude: The same trade the course gives a move later, after 7...O-O 8.O-O d5.
- 8...cxd5 claude: Black recaptures.
- 9.O-O claude: We castle. After 9...O-O it is the position of 7...O-O 8.O-O d5 9.exd5 cxd5.
- 9...O-O claude: Black castles too.
- 10.Bg5 White has a good choice of moves here. I suggest this one, again setting up an annoying pin.

7...d5, opening the center, is the most reliable defense for Black.

front.text: After 10.Bg5, what is your plan, and what speaks for our position?

cards.back:
We want to increase the pressure on Black's kingside (Qf3 is a key idea) and use the open e-file.

All of our pieces enjoy active positions, and our pawn structure is ideal, without any weaknesses.

front.text: What is your move after 7...O-O, and what are Black's 2 main moves after it?

cards.back:
8.O-O claude: We castle as well.

- [8...d5] opens the center, the same reliable defense as 7...d5.
- [8...Re8] is a better try for Black than taking on c3.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 8...d5 ?

cards.back:
- 9.exd5 claude: We take the pawn, and the trade opens the e-file.
- 9...cxd5 claude: Black recaptures.
- 10.Bg5 White has a good choice of moves; I suggest this one, again setting up an annoying pin. claude: It is the same position as after 7...d5 8.exd5 cxd5 9.O-O O-O 10.Bg5.

front.text: What are the next 9 plies following 8...Re8 ?

cards.back:
- 9.Bg5! sets up an annoying pin again.
- 9...h6 claude: Black hits the bishop.
- 10.Bh4 claude: We keep the pin.
- 10...g5 claude: Black breaks the pin, at the cost of weakening the king.
- 11.Bg3 claude: The bishop's only retreat.
- 11...Bxc3 claude: Black takes the knight that guards e4.
- 12.bxc3 claude: We recapture.
- 12...Nxe4 claude: Black wins the e-pawn, the point of chasing our bishop away.
- 13.Qh5! gives us a strong attack against Black's weakened king.

front.text: Black doubles your pawns with 7...Bxc3+?! Do you need to worry, and why?

cards.back:
8.bxc3 A questionable trade for Black. Our pawn structure is damaged, but our dark-squared bishop gains in strength now.

- [8...O-O] is the better choice.
- [8...d5]? would be a complete disaster.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 8...O-O, and why is the pin so annoying?

cards.back:
- 9.O-O claude: We castle as well.
- 9...d6 claude: Black opens the diagonal for the c8-bishop.
- 10.Bg5! shows the second annoying post for our bishop. We pin Black's knight, and it is tough for Black to untangle. They can play ...h6 & ...g5, but the 'cure' would be worse than the disease − Black's king won't be happy about it!

front.text: After 8...d5?, what are the next 3 plies?

cards.back:
- 9.exd5 claude: We open the e-file.
- 9...cxd5 claude: Black recaptures.
- 10.Ba3! Black can't castle. This would be a complete disaster, so 8...O-O is a better choice.

It illustrates how our dark-squared bishop gains in strength after the trade on c3.

front.text: What do you play after 6...Bxc3+?! and where does it lead?

cards.back:
7.bxc3 claude: We recapture. After [7...bxc6 8.Bd3] it is the same position as after 6...bxc6 7.Bd3 Bxc3+ 8.bxc3.

6...Bxc3+?! surrenders the bishop pair prematurely.

front.text: What do you play after 6...dxc6?! and why?

cards.back: 7.Qxd8+ Black gives up castling rights for no benefit.

front.text: What is the conclusion on 5...Bb4! and on the whole chapter?

cards.back:
Black's absolute best way to play after 1.e4 e5 is entering the Four Knights 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 and then answer 4.d4 with 4...exd4 5.Nxd4 Bb4!, as examined in the main line of the current chapter. In this case, Black has good chances to equalize the game.

We still have no reasons to complain, as our position allows us to develop the pieces to active squares, our pawn structure is sound, and our king is secure.

In practice, Black will often choose a different path. The current chapter shows that Black can't get equal chances in these cases and often gets in serious trouble quickly.

front.text: How good is 5...Bc5 for Black, in theory and in practice?

cards.back:
Black opts for a natural development move and attacks our centralized knight. This move can't be bad, and its theoretical evaluation is 'slightly better for White', not more.

However, this is based on the assumption of close-to-perfect play afterwards. In practice, Black often stumbles right on the next move.

front.text: What is your move after 5...Bc5 and why? How is it different from 5...Bb4! ?

cards.back: 6.Be3! It is important to remember this move. After 5...Bb4! we must play 6.Nxc6, which is the only good option. Here, after the bishop comes to c5, we have the additional option to cover the knight, which is considerably stronger and gives Black plenty of options to go wrong.

front.text: After 6.Be3!, what do we threaten?

cards.back: Our move might look innocent, but Black's bishop is unprotected. This makes Nxc6! a serious threat!

front.text: What are Black's 4 main moves after 6.Be3! and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [6...Nxd4]?! (or the similar [6...Bxd4]) is great for White.
- [6...Bb6]! is best, retreating the bishop to a safe square.
- [6...O-O]?? ignores our idea.
- [6...d6]? covers the bishop, but it is still a big mistake.

front.text: After 6...Nxd4?!, what are the next 3 plies, and what is the plan?

cards.back:
- 7.Bxd4 claude: We take back with the bishop, which the queen guards.
- 7...Bxd4 claude: Black trades bishops.
- 8.Qxd4 is great for White. We are ready to castle queenside and launch a kingside pawn storm (f3 & g4 & h5), a familiar idea.

The similar [6...Bxd4 7.Bxd4 Nxd4 8.Qxd4] claude: reaches the same position.

front.text: What are the next 5 plies following 6...Bb6!, and how do we stand?

cards.back:
- 7.Qd2 Going for queenside castling.
- 7...O-O claude: Black castles.
- 8.O-O-O claude: As planned.
- 8...Re8 claude: Black attacks the e4-pawn a second time.
- 9.f3 We have the better chances, but Black's position is viable. The move not only covers our pawn but may also be the start of the kingside pawn storm, based on g2-g4-g5.

6...Bb6! is best, retreating the bishop to a safe square.

front.text: After 6...O-O??, what are the next 3 plies?

cards.back:
- 7.Nxc6! Black ignored our idea.
- 7...bxc6 claude: Black recaptures, but the bishop on c5 is left hanging.
- 8.Bxc5 wins a piece.

front.text: After 6...d6?, what are the next 7 plies, and how do we stand?

cards.back:
- 7.Nxc6 6...d6? covers the bishop, but it is still a big mistake.
- 7...bxc6 claude: Black recaptures.
- 8.Bxc5 claude: We trade bishops; the recapture ruins Black's pawns and opens the d-file.
- 8...dxc5 claude: Black takes back, and the d-file opens.
- 9.Qxd8+ claude: We trade queens, and only the king can take back.
- 9...Kxd8 claude: Forced.
- 10.O-O-O+ We reach a fantastic endgame. Black has the weakest pawn structure you can imagine.

front.text: Besides 4...exd4, which 2 Black replies to 4.d4 do we look at, and how do we feel about them?

cards.back:
Black's best reply to 4.d4 is 4...exd4. Two alternatives are worth checking:

- [4...Bb4] pins our knight, but it is a risky choice. We need to know how to tackle it though.
- [4...d6] is a passive defense but important to study. The resulting positions may also arise from different move orders.

Other moves make little sense, as we attack the e-pawn, and Black can't just ignore this threat.

front.text: What is your move after 4...Bb4 and why?

cards.back:
5.Nxe5! The only good move! White often struggles against 4...Bb4 because it is not obvious at first sight why you should capture e5 with the knight and avoid other options.

4...Bb4 is a rare and slightly dubious move. We can prove an advantage, but only with this one reply!

front.text: After 4...Bb4, why not 5.dxe5 or 5.d5 ?

cards.back:
- [5.dxe5]? The problem with [5.dxe5 | 5...Nxe4] is that Black immediately puts serious pressure on our c3-knight.
- Black is also happy about [5.d5 Ne7 6.Nxe5 Nxe4], when the pin is annoying again.

front.text: What are Black's 2 main moves after 5.Nxe5! and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [5...Nxe4] is Black's most aggressive reply. Black wants to get the pawn back immediately. It's not a good move, but it requires a precise reply.
- [5...Nxe5]? is an even worse option.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 5...Nxe4, and why is Black's reply forced?

cards.back:
- 6.Qg4! The best and most fun move to play! We attack both the knight and the g-pawn and enter wild complications.
- 6...Nxc3 was the only move available. The knight was attacked, and retreating or covering it failed due to our queen taking g7.
- 7.Qxg7! Wow, what a mess! The position is very favorable for us.

front.text: What are Black's 3 main moves after 7.Qxg7! and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [7...Nd5+ 8.c3] or [7...Ne4+ 8.c3] is great for us.
- [7...Rf8] leads to an even more exciting position.

front.text: What are the next 5 plies following 7...Nd5+ (or 7...Ne4+), and how do we stand after them?

cards.back:
- 8.c3 We still attack the h8-rook and threaten mate, which will win back the piece with interest.
- 8...Qf6 claude: Black offers a queen trade.
- 9.Qxf6 claude: We trade queens.
- 9...Nxf6 claude: Black recaptures.
- 10.Nxc6 claude: We take the knight, and the bishop on b4 is still attacked by our c-pawn.

[7...Ne4+ 8.c3] is the same. After [10...Bxc3+ 11.bxc3] we have great bishops in a wide-open position.

front.text: What is your move after 7...Rf8, and what are Black's 2 main moves after it?

cards.back:
8.a3! attacks Black's bishop.

- [8...Ba5] The bishop retreats.
- [8...Nxd4] is even wilder.

front.text: What are the next 7 plies following 8...Ba5, and how do we stand?

cards.back:
- 9.Nxc6 claude: We trade knights with an attack on the queen.
- 9...dxc6 claude: Black recaptures.
- 10.Qe5+ claude: A check that also hits the bishop on a5.
- 10...Qe7 claude: Black blocks the check with the queen.
- 11.Qxe7+ claude: Our queen is pinned, so we trade.
- 11...Kxe7 claude: Forced.
- 12.Bd2! gives us a large advantage after regaining the piece.

front.text: What are the next 5 plies following 8...Nxd4, and what do we threaten?

cards.back:
- 9.axb4! claude: We take the bishop and leave the knights alone.
- 9...Nxc2+ claude: Black forks king and rook.
- 10.Kd2 claude: The king attacks both knights.
- 10...Nxa1 claude: Black takes the rook.
- 11.Kxc3! We have a winning attack! The main threat is Bc4 and Re1, aiming for the king!

It is funny to see our king on c3 and the stranded enemy knight on a1, but this is irrelevant, as we strike first.

front.text: After 5...Nxe5?, what are the next 9 plies?

cards.back:
- 6.dxe5 claude: We recapture and attack the knight.
- 6...Nxe4 claude: Black takes the e-pawn, as in the main line.
- 7.Qg4! is great for us.
- 7...Nxc3 claude: Black takes our knight.
- 8.Qxb4! claude: With our d-pawn gone from d4, the queen can take the bishop.
- 8...Nd5 claude: The knight escapes with an attack on our queen.
- 9.Qg4 − how does Black defend the kingside?
- 9...O-O claude: Black castles to cover g7.
- 10.Bh6 We win material. claude: Mate on g7 is threatened, and after 10...g6 the bishop takes the rook on f8.

5...Nxe5? is an even worse option than 5...Nxe4.

front.text: What is the verdict on the whole 4...Bb4 5.Nxe5 Nxe4 variation?

cards.back: It is rarely played and extremely dubious for Black, but we need to be ready for a wild game. Studying the complications is lots of fun, even if you'll rarely get it on the board in a real game.

front.text: Why is 4...d6 important to study, although it is passive and dubious?

cards.back:
The position after 4...d6 and the following line may arise from various move orders, making it a fairly frequently seen line if you add up all the possible ways to reach it:

- [1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nc6 4.Nc3 Nf6]
- [1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 d6 4.d4 Nf6]
- [1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Nf3 Nc6]

Whenever Black opts for an early ...Nc6 and ...d6, locking in their f8-bishop, we'll reach similar or identical positions.

front.text: What is your move after 4...d6 and why?

cards.back: 5.Bb5! An important move to remember! We pin Black's knight and thus increase the pressure on the e5-pawn. In addition, we also threaten d4-d5, attacking the unlucky pinned knight!

front.text: After 4...d6, why not trade on e5 ?

cards.back:
We don't want to trade on e5, as Black is happy about the simplifications. After [5.dxe5 Nxe5 6.Nxe5 dxe5 7.Qxd8+ Kxd8], we could spoil Black's castling ideas, but once the queens are traded, this is less of a problem for our opponent.

Ultimately, we only helped Black because the trades activated their f8-bishop. We want to keep this piece locked in and, therefore, should avoid the capture on e5.

front.text: What are Black's 2 main moves after 5.Bb5! and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
The pin and the threat of d4-d5 only leave two options for Black:

- [5...Bd7] breaks the pin, a logical move.
- [5...exd4] takes the pawn on d4. Black gives up the idea of keeping a pawn on e5.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 5...Bd7 ?

cards.back:
- 6.Bxc6! This move is surprisingly strong, although we give up the bishop for a knight voluntarily.
- 6...Bxc6 The only good reply. Black must play it to set up a counterattack on our e-pawn.
- 7.Qe2! A strong move! We cover the attacked e-pawn and accomplish several points. Black's e-pawn is now in danger again.

front.text: After 6.Bxc6!, why must Black take back with the bishop?

cards.back:
[6...Bxc6] is the only good reply, as [6...bxc6]? [6...bxc6 | 7.dxe5] wins the e-pawn for us.

Black must play 6...Bxc6 to set up a counterattack on our e-pawn.

front.text: After 6...Bxc6, why not 7.dxe5 ?

cards.back: [7.dxe5]? is bad due to [7.dxe5 | 7...Nxe4], when we have achieved nothing.

front.text: What are Black's 3 main moves after 7.Qe2! and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [7...exd4] is Black's most common and relatively best continuation.
- [7...Be7]? Black can't just play 'any move', as [7...Be7 | 8.dxe5] demonstrates.
- [7...Nd7]?? tries to cover the pawn, but we trap the bishop.

front.text: What is your move after 7...exd4, and where does it lead?

cards.back: 8.Nxd4 leads to a position that we examine via the more common move order 5...exd4 6.Nxd4 Bd7 7.Bxc6 Bxc6 8.Qe2, which is excellent for White.

front.text: What do you play after 7...Be7? and why?

cards.back: 8.dxe5 Black's e-pawn was in danger again, and they can't just play 'any move'. claude: We win a pawn.

front.text: What do you play after 7...Nd7?? and why?

cards.back: 8.d5! traps the bishop!

front.text: After 5...Be7??, what are the next 7 plies?

cards.back:
- 6.d5 Black can't ignore the pin. claude: We attack the pinned knight.
- 6...a6 claude: Black hits the bishop to break the pin.
- 7.Ba4 claude: We keep the pin.
- 7...b5 claude: Black hits the bishop again.
- 8.Nxb5! claude: We give the knight to keep the pin.
- 8...axb5 claude: Black takes it.
- 9.Bxb5 We'll regain the piece with interest.

front.text: After 5...a6??, what are the next 3 plies?

cards.back:
- 6.Bxc6+ claude: We take with check.
- 6...bxc6 claude: Black recaptures.
- 7.dxe5 We win the central pawn and have weakened Black's pawn structure on top of that.

front.text: What is your move after 5...exd4, and why does it leave Black little choice?

cards.back:
6.Nxd4 We are now attacking Black's knight twice, so there is little choice for our opponent.

With 5...exd4 Black gives up the idea of keeping a pawn on e5.

front.text: Which other move orders reach the position after 5...exd4 6.Nxd4 ?

cards.back:
- [4...exd4 5.Nxd4 d6 6.Bb5]
- [1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3 Nc6 6.Bb5]

front.text: What are the next 7 plies following 6...Bd7, and what are we ready for?

cards.back:
- 7.Bxc6! A strong move! Usually, you want to keep your pair of bishops − this case is an exception. By taking on c6, we preserve our well-placed d4-knight.
- 7...Bxc6 This recapture is played most of the time.
- 8.Qe2 We cover our important central pawn and prepare Bf4 and O-O-O.
- 8...Be7 claude: Black develops.
- 9.Bf4 claude: The bishop comes out, as 8.Qe2 prepared.
- 9...O-O claude: Black castles.
- 10.O-O-O We are ready to launch a kingside attack based on moves like g4 and Nf5. Black has no counterplay to speak of.

With 6...Bd7 Black needs to cover the knight; there is nothing else.

front.text: Why is the position after 8.Qe2 of special importance?

cards.back: [5...Bd7 6.Bxc6 Bxc6 7.Qe2 exd4 8.Nxd4] is a second move order to reach it. Black is in trouble now, as our simple plan is very effective.

front.text: Why can we afford to castle queenside against Black's setup with 4...d6 ?

cards.back:
Black's setup, starting with 4...d6, is passive. This allows us to play more ambitiously than usual. Going for queenside castling is a promising option here, as it allows us to have a safe king and still push the kingside pawns forward to start an attack.

In many opening lines, it is not feasible to castle queenside, as it takes too much time to prepare. Black's passive setup gives us the time to play Qe2, Bf4 and finally, O-O-O.

front.text: What are the next 5 plies following 7...bxc6 ?

cards.back:
- 8.Qf3! accomplishes multiple goals. We prepare queenside castling, strengthen Nf5 ideas, and we are ready to answer 8...Be7 with 9.e5!
- 8...Be7 claude: Black develops.
- 9.e5! claude: We open the long diagonal for our queen.
- 9...dxe5 claude: Black takes the pawn.
- 10.Nxc6 leads to a crushing attack.

front.text: What do you play after 6...a6?? and why?

cards.back: 7.Nxc6! wins even more material than the other capture, [7.Bxc6+].

front.text: What is the conclusion on Black's alternatives to 4...exd4 ?

cards.back: Black should answer 4.d4 with 4...exd4, as the alternatives don't convince. The pin 4...Bb4 leads to tactical complications, but Black is in danger. On the other hand, 4...d6 is too passive and gives us excellent prospects for an attack.

front.text: How good is 2...Nc6 against the Alapin, and what does Black need?

cards.back:
Black develops the knight, a logical move. It follows general opening principles and can't be bad.

A closer look reveals that it is objectively fine, but Black needs to know or find the correct path on the next moves, or they will get in trouble.

front.text: What is your move after 2...Nc6 and why?

cards.back: 3.d4 That was our plan: build a perfect pawn center. Now we get to the first crucial moment.

front.text: What are Black's 3 main moves after 3.d4, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [3...cxd4] In practice, Black usually trades on d4, which is less precise.
- [3...e6]? is a mistake. The move ...e6 is common in the Sicilian, but mistimed here.
- [3...d5]! Black's best reply is rarely played. [3...d5 | 4.exd5 Qxd5] transposes to a viable main line for Black.

front.text: What is your move after 3...d5! and where does it lead?

cards.back:
4.exd5 Qxd5 transposes to a position we examine via [2...d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.d4 Nc6], a viable main line for Black.

3...d5! is Black's best reply, but it is rarely played.

front.text: What is your move after 3...cxd4, and why are we happy about the trade?

cards.back:
4.cxd4 And we have reached the second critical position of this line.

3...cxd4 is a natural move, but we are always happy about this trade, as we are granted the additional option Nc3.

front.text: What are Black's 3 main moves after 4.cxd4, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
