- [4...d5] is Black's only way to a reasonable game. It transposes to a line we cover in a different chapter, and it is still Black's best option.
- [4...e6]?! If they don't play 4...d5, they are in trouble.
- [4...d6]?! A passive move that does not fight for an equal share of the center.

front.text: What is your move after 4...d5, and where does it lead?

cards.back: 5.exd5 Qxd5 6.Nf3 transposes to the variation [2...d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.d4 cxd4 5.cxd4 Nc6 6.Nf3], which we cover in a different chapter. We have better chances in this line, but it is still Black's best option.

front.text: What is your move after 4...e6?! and why is it better than 5.Nf3 ?

cards.back:
5.d5! We gain more space with a tempo gain.

This move is a lot stronger than [5.Nf3], when [5.Nf3 | 5...d5] is reasonable for Black.

front.text: What are Black's 2 main moves after 5.d5! and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [5...exd5] Black usually takes on d5.
- [5...Ne5] is possible, too. We have a nice advantage against it after many moves.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 5...exd5 ?

cards.back:
- 6.exd5 claude: We take back and keep a pawn on d5.
- 6...Ne5 Not [6...Nce7]?? [6...Nce7 | 7.d6 Ng6 8.Qe2+], winning a piece.
- 7.Nf3 This simple move speeds up our development.

front.text: After 6...Ne5, why 7.Nf3 and not 7.Qe2 ?

cards.back:
[7.Nf3] This simple move speeds up our development.

I'm not too fond of [7.Qe2 Qe7], as our kingside development is just as hampered as Black's.

front.text: After 7.Nf3, how do we stand and why?

cards.back: After the healthy 7.Nf3, we have some advantage. The pawn on d5 gives us more space, and we are the first to castle and use the e-file.

front.text: After 6...Nce7??, what are the next 3 plies?

cards.back:
- 7.d6 claude: The pawn hits the knight on e7.
- 7...Ng6 claude: The knight has to move.
- 8.Qe2+ winning a piece. claude: Every block loses a piece: on e7 the d6-pawn takes it, and a knight on e5 falls to our queen.

front.text: Which 3 moves give us a nice advantage after 5...Ne5 ?

cards.back:
We have a nice advantage against it after many moves, like [6.Nc3], [6.Nf3], or the aggressive [6.f4] − a matter of taste.

5...Ne5 is possible, but Black usually takes on d5.

front.text: What is the conclusion on 2...Nc6 ?

cards.back: Black often plays 2...Nc6 without any concrete knowledge and gets into serious trouble. The move is not bad, but Black needs to transpose to [2...d5] lines quickly. As we have witnessed in this chapter, anything else is excellent for White.

front.text: After 4...d6?!, what are the next 3 plies?

cards.back:
- 5.d5! Gaining space and time.
- 5...Ne5 claude: The attacked knight goes to the center.
- 6.f4 The most aggressive way. There is nothing wrong about [6.Nc3] or a similar development, but our pawn center looks crushing after pushing the f-pawn.

4...d6?! is a passive move that does not fight for an equal share of the center.

front.text: After 6.f4, what is our plan once Black's knight retreats, and why is Black struggling?

cards.back:
After Black retreats their knight, we will develop our knights to f3 and c3, and prepare kingside castling next.

Black has difficulty developing, as their pieces stand on each other's toes.

front.text: Which 2 moves are good after 6...Ng6, and does the order matter?

cards.back:
[7.Nc3] is a good move, but [7.Nf3] is just as good. We want to develop the two knights to their most active squares and the order is not important.

Black is in severe trouble now, as they can't develop their kingside easily.

front.text: What are Black's 2 main moves after 7.Nc3, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [7...Nf6] [7...Nf6 | 8.Nf3 e5 9.dxe6 fxe6 10.Bc4] is awkward for Black, as their central pawns are weak and the king won't be able to castle easily.
- [7...e5] [7...e5 | 8.dxe6 fxe6 9.Nf3] likely transposes to the 7...Nf6 line. Black has no good way to develop the kingside without moving the e-pawn, which will create weaknesses.

front.text: What are the next 7 plies following 7...Nf6, what does our first move threaten, and how do we stand?

cards.back:
- 8.Nf3 We threaten e4-e5 now! claude: The pawn would hit the knight on f6.
- 8...e5 claude: Black stops e4-e5.
- 9.dxe6 claude: We take en passant.
- 9...fxe6 claude: Black recaptures.
- 10.Bc4 is awkward for Black, as their central pawns are weak and the king won't be able to castle easily.
- 10...Be7 claude: Black develops.
- 11.Nd4 Black has no satisfactory move. claude: Knight and bishop now both hit the e6-pawn.

Or [8...e6 9.dxe6 fxe6 10.Bc4], the same position.

front.text: After 7...e5, what are the next 3 plies?

cards.back:
- 8.dxe6 claude: We take en passant.
- 8...fxe6 claude: Black recaptures.
- 9.Nf3 likely transposes to the 7...Nf6 line. Black has no good way to develop the kingside without moving the e-pawn, which will create weaknesses.

front.text: What is your move after 3...e6? and why?

cards.back:
4.d5 Of course. We are happy to gain more space in the center and push around Black's knight.

3...e6? The move ...e6 is common in the Sicilian, but mistimed here.

front.text: Why is Black even worse off here than in the similar line 3...cxd4 4.cxd4 e6 5.d5 ?

cards.back: This line is similar to [3...cxd4 4.cxd4 e6 5.d5], but Black is in even worse shape here. The pawn on c5 worsens the situation for the f8-bishop.

front.text: What are Black's 2 main moves after 4.d5, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [4...exd5] claude: The main line; it ends in a large advantage for us.
- [4...Ne5]? [4...Ne5 | 5.f4 Ng6 6.d6] looks even worse. How does Black ever get developed?

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 4...exd5 ?

cards.back:
- 5.exd5 claude: We take back and keep a pawn on d5.
- 5...Ne5 Black has to avoid [5...Nce7]?? [5...Nce7 | 6.d6 Ng6 7.Qe2+], winning us a piece!
- 6.Nf3 The simplest solution to get castled quickly.

front.text: After 6...Nxf3+ 7.Qxf3, how do we stand, and where do our pieces belong?

cards.back:
White has a large advantage. We have much more space due to the advanced d-pawn, giving us good spots for our pieces. The bishops would be well-placed on d3 and f4, while c4 looks like a good knight outpost.

The easy development helps with castling kingside quickly. This also means that we will be faster in using the only open file − a very nice opening result.

front.text: After 5...Nce7??, what are the next 3 plies?

cards.back:
- 6.d6 claude: The pawn hits the knight on e7.
- 6...Ng6 claude: The knight has to move.
- 7.Qe2+ winning us a piece! claude: Every block loses a piece: on e7 the d6-pawn takes it, and a knight on e5 falls to our queen.

front.text: After 4...Ne5?, what are the next 3 plies?

cards.back:
- 5.f4 claude: The pawn chases the knight.
- 5...Ng6 claude: The knight retreats.
- 6.d6 looks even worse for Black. How does Black ever get developed? The d6-pawn is a real pain!

front.text: What is Black's idea with 2...d6 against the Alapin, and does it stop us?

cards.back:
Black goes for 2...d6, which prepares the attack on our e-pawn with ...Nf6. Black argues that [2...Nf6] is answered by [2...Nf6 | 3.e5], so they want to prepare the knight jump by covering the e5-square.

This concept makes sense but does not stop us from building and maintaining the strong pawn duo e4&d4.

front.text: What is your move after 2...d6 and why?

cards.back: 3.d4 Easy, that was our idea: building and maintaining the strong pawn duo e4&d4.

front.text: What are Black's 2 main moves after 3.d4, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [3...Nf6] Black attacks our e-pawn, the idea of the previous move.
- [3...cxd4] Black also frequently inserts the trade and then plays ...Nf6: [3...cxd4 | 4.cxd4 Nf6 5.Bd3] leads to the positions of our main line.

front.text: What is your move after 3...cxd4, and where does it lead?

cards.back: 4.cxd4 and then 4...Nf6, when 5.Bd3 leads to the positions of our main line [3...Nf6 4.Bd3 cxd4 5.cxd4]. This position frequently arises this way, when Black has traded the pawns one move earlier.

front.text: What is your move after 3...Nf6 and why?

cards.back: 4.Bd3 We cover our central pawn and get one move closer to kingside castling. This move looks very logical and leads to positions that are simple to play.

front.text: What are Black's 2 main moves after 4.Bd3, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [4...cxd4] Black's usual choice.
- [4...g6] They can also delay the capture and play something like 4...g6, when [4...g6 | 5.Nf3] and a quick O-O completes our kingside development. Black will usually take on d4 at some point, transposing to our main line.

front.text: What is your move after 4...g6, and where does it lead?

cards.back:
5.Nf3 and a quick O-O completes our kingside development.

Black will usually take on d4 at some point, transposing to our main line of the current chapter.

front.text: What is your move after 4...cxd4, and by which other move order is this position often reached?

cards.back: 5.cxd4 This position frequently arises via the move order [3...cxd4 4.cxd4 Nf6 5.Bd3], when Black has traded the pawns one move earlier.

front.text: What are Black's 2 main moves after 5.cxd4, and what do they aim at?

cards.back:
- [5...g6] Black opts for the kingside fianchetto. This setup makes great sense, as the g7-bishop will be aimed at our d4-pawn.
- [5...Nc6] Black attacks our unprotected d-pawn.

front.text: What is your move after 5...g6 and why?

cards.back:
6.Nf3 A natural move that protects the d4-pawn and gets us one move closer to kingside castling.

5...g6 aims the g7-bishop at our d4-pawn. Currently, this pawn is undefended and could be a potential target for Black.

front.text: What are Black's 2 main moves after 6.Nf3, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [6...Bg7] A very natural move.
- [6...Bg4] pinning our knight. A strong reply is [6...Bg4 | 7.Nbd2]!, anticipating the capture of our knight.

front.text: What is your move after 6...Bg7, and what do we need to watch?

cards.back:
7.O-O We castle, as planned.

Black has one viable target, our d4-pawn. We need to be a bit careful about it.

front.text: What are Black's 2 main moves after 7.O-O, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [7...O-O] is the most natural move. Now I suggest investing some time to play [7...O-O | 8.h3]!, which stops Black's pinning idea ...Bg4.
- [7...Bg4] is possible, setting up the pin before we play h3. We have a good reply, the move [7...Bg4 | 8.Nbd2].

front.text: What is your move after 7...O-O, and why not the standard 8.Nc3 ?

cards.back:
8.h3! stops Black's pinning idea ...Bg4. After h3 is on the board, we can continue with Nc3 and Be3, and complete our development.

[8.Nc3]?! This standard move is not optimal. [8.Nc3 | 8...Bg4]! Attacking the d-pawn by pinning.

front.text: After 8.Nc3?! Bg4! 9.Be3 Nc6 10.h3?! Bxf3 11.Qxf3, how does Black hit our d-pawn?

cards.back:
[11...Nd7]!, when Black has generated a strong attack on our d-pawn. [11...Nd7 | 12.Ne2]? even fails to [11...Nd7 12.Ne2 | 12...Nde5]!, winning a pawn for Black!

This line is far from the best play by White, but it illustrates Black's basic ideas.

front.text: What is your move after 7...Bg4 and why?

cards.back:
8.Nbd2 allows us to answer ...Bxf3 with Nxf3, keeping d4 nicely covered.

After 8...O-O 9.h3 Bxf3 10.Nxf3, our chances are excellent. Our center is stable, and we enjoy the pair of bishops.

front.text: What is your move after 6...Bg4 and why?

cards.back: 7.Nbd2! anticipating the capture of our knight. It allows us to answer ...Bxf3 with Nxf3, keeping d4 nicely covered.

front.text: What are our 2 ways to meet ...Bg4 against Black's ...g6 setup?

cards.back:
We need to either play an early h3 to stop ...Bg4, or we need to be able to answer ...Bg4 with Nbd2.

It is perfectly possible for us to play [7.h3] or even [6.h3] to prevent any ...Bg4 ideas. It is not necessary though. As long as we can answer ...Bg4 with Nbd2, developing the kingside and castling is just as good.

front.text: What is the conclusion on 2...d6 ?

cards.back:
Black's opening concept does not stop our intention to build a strong center. We have good chances for an advantage based on our excellent central control.

Black has some ideas to attack our center (...Bg4, ...Nc6), and it's instructive to study how to fight them effectively. Model game: J. van Foreest − A. Fedorov.

front.text: What is your move after 5...Nc6, and is 6.d5 a mistake?

cards.back:
6.Nf3 I suggest covering the pawn, but [6.d5] is not a mistake. We gain a lot of space, and Black's knight has to move again. I still prefer 6.Nf3 though. We keep a strong central pawn duo and may still advance one of the pawns later.

5...Nc6 attacks our unprotected d-pawn.

front.text: What are Black's 2 main moves after 6.Nf3, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [6...Bg4] A natural move, pinning our knight. As a consequence, our d-pawn is now hanging.
- [6...g6] An alternative for Black, when [6...g6 | 7.h3] leads to a position that we examine via [5...g6 6.Nf3], the current chapter's main line.

front.text: What is your move after 6...Bg4, and why not 7.d5 ?

cards.back:
7.Be3 Again, I prefer to cover the center and not advance the d-pawn.

I think [7.d5 Bxf3 8.Qxf3 Ne5] allows Black some trades and helps them to organize.

6...Bg4 pins our knight. As a consequence, our d-pawn is now hanging.

front.text: What are Black's 2 main moves after 7.Be3, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
Black needs to decide how to develop their kingside.

- [7...g6] I suggest [7...g6 | 8.Nbd2], an idea that we employ in the 5...g6 variation too.
- [7...e6] is a different idea. Black's bishop will be less active on e7, which gives us more choices. We have some advantage due to our strong center.

front.text: What is your move after 7...g6 and why?

cards.back: 8.Nbd2, an idea that we employ in the 5...g6 variation too. It allows us to answer ...Bxf3 with Nxf3, keeping d4 nicely covered.

front.text: Which 2 moves are good after 7...e6, and why do we have more choices?

cards.back:
We could play [8.Nc3] or [8.O-O], for example. Black's bishop will be less active on e7, which gives us more choices.

We have some advantage due to our strong center.

front.text: What is your move after 6...g6, and where does it lead?

cards.back:
7.h3 leads to a position that we examine via [5...g6 6.Nf3], the current chapter's main line.

We need to either play an early h3 to stop ...Bg4, or we need to be able to answer ...Bg4 with Nbd2.

front.text: What is Black's idea with 2...e6 against the Alapin?

cards.back: Black prepares the move ...d5, an idea similar to the French Defense. It is no surprise that the following lines feature multiple possible transpositions to this opening or its typical structures.

front.text: What is your move after 2...e6 and why?

cards.back: 3.d4 The automatic reply, completing our central pawn duo.

front.text: What are Black's 5 main moves after 3.d4, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [3...cxd4]?! A common reply. It is premature and helps our cause by allowing Nc3 soon.
- [3...d5] Black's only fully satisfactory move.
- [3...Nc6]? Black sometimes goes for it. Then [3...Nc6 | 4.d5], which we cover in our chapter on 2...Nc6.
- [3...d6] A passive move, best answered by a natural setup of Nf3, Bd3, and O-O.
- [3...b6] Passive too, met by the same setup.

front.text: What is your move after 3...Nc6? and why?

cards.back:
4.d5 We are happy to gain more space in the center and push around Black's knight.

We cover this position in our chapter on 2...Nc6, via [2...Nc6 3.d4 e6].

front.text: What setup do we choose against the passive 3...d6 or 3...b6 ?

cards.back: Passive moves like 3...d6 or [3...b6] are best answered by a natural setup of Nf3, Bd3, and O-O.

front.text: What is your move after 3...cxd4?! and why are we happy about the trade?

cards.back: 4.cxd4 As always, we are happy about this trade. After our natural reply, we'll gain the c3-square for our knight.

front.text: What are Black's 4 main moves after 4.cxd4, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [4...d5] This is best. Black needs a pawn on a central square, attacking our e-pawn.
- [4...Nc6]? Then [4...Nc6 | 5.d5], which we examine in the chapter on 2...Nc6. White is much better.
- [4...Bb4+] I also found some games featuring it. Best answered by developing with Nc3 and Bd3, preparing kingside castling.
- [4...Nf6] The same: we develop with Nc3 and Bd3, preparing kingside castling.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 4...d5, and what is our goal?

cards.back:
- 5.e5! I suggest advancing the pawn. Without the c-pawns, we can develop our queen's knight to its most active square on c3. After the premature trade of the c-pawns, we always have the excellent c3-square for our knight to enter the game.
- 5...Nc6 is the most popular and best move. Black wants to put pressure on our d-pawn. They can increase it with a later ...Qb6 or ...Ne7-f5.
- 6.Nf3 The best square for our knight. We cover d4 and prepare kingside castling. Our goal is to keep our d-pawn safely protected, and seek to exploit our advantage in space.

4...d5 is best. Black needs a pawn on a central square, attacking our e-pawn.

front.text: After 4...d5, why not 5.exd5 or 5.Nc3 ?

cards.back:
Going for [5.exd5 exd5] is toothless, as the position is completely symmetrical. After [5.Nc3 dxe4], Black is fine too.

With c-pawns on the board, in the French, I recommend 3.exd5 exd5 4.c4, putting pressure on d5. This concept doesn't work here in the Sicilian for obvious reasons: the c-pawns are already traded.

front.text: After 5.e5!, why is this an improved French Advance for us?

cards.back:
Compared to the French Advance (1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5), the c-pawns are gone. In the French, you could reach the position via 3...c5 4.c3 cxd4?! 5.cxd4, but it is a dubious line: Black can wait until White has chosen a worse square for the knight (like a3) and only trade on d4 if desired.

Black started with 1...c5, not 1...e6 − they will likely not know these positions well. It gives us a good opportunity to play this pawn structure under particularly favorable conditions.

front.text: What are Black's 3 main moves after 6.Nf3, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [6...Qb6] looks sensible, to put more pressure on d4. Now [6...Qb6 | 7.Nc3] is a good reply.
- [6...Nge7] is an interesting line. Black wants ...Nf5 and ...Qb6, attacking our pawn even more. A strong reply is similar to the 6...Qb6 line: Nc3 and a3!
- [6...Bb4+]? A popular but bad move, frequently seen below the master level. The fundamental problem of Black's concept is the bishop's placement on b4.

front.text: What are the next 7 plies following 6...Qb6 ?

cards.back:
- 7.Nc3 It not only develops a piece but will often be useful to start an attack on the queenside.
- 7...Bd7 claude: Black develops and makes room for ...Rc8.
- 8.a3! preparing Na4.
- 8...Rc8 claude: Black brings the rook to the c-file.
- 9.Na4 claude: The knight hits the queen on b6.
- 9...Qc7 claude: The queen retreats.
- 10.Bd3 and we are much better.

front.text: After 10.Bd3, how do we stand and what is our plan?

cards.back: We are much better. A later b2-b4 gives us an excellent game on the queenside.

front.text: What are the next 7 plies following 6...Nge7 ?

cards.back:
- 7.Nc3 claude: We develop, as against 6...Qb6.
- 7...Nf5 Black wants to play ...Qb6 next, attacking our pawn even more.
- 8.a3! A strong reply, similar to the 6...Qb6 line.
- 8...Qb6 claude: Black piles up on d4.
- 9.Na4! sending the queen to a passive square.
- 9...Qa5+? claude: The queen comes out with check.
- 10.b4, rendering Black's concept a complete failure. We needed to play the move a3 to enable this.

front.text: What are the next 5 plies following 6...Bb4+?, and what is wrong with Black's bishop?

cards.back:
- 7.Nc3 claude: We block the check with a developing move.
- 7...Nge7 claude: Black develops.
- 8.Bd3 claude: Our bishop aims at h7.
- 8...O-O?? A striking example of the bishop missing as a defender of the kingside.
- 9.Bxh7+! is already 'Lights Out!' for Black. The 'Greek Gift', as we call it, is a common attacking idea in French structures.

The fundamental problem of Black's concept is the bishop's placement on b4. Taking our knight looks unattractive... so what is the bishop doing on b4? An additional problem: the bishop may be a useful defender of the kingside.

front.text: What is your move after 4...Nc6? and why?

cards.back:
5.d5 We gain more space with a tempo gain. White is much better.

We examine this position in the chapter on 2...Nc6, via [2...Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.cxd4 e6].

front.text: What is your move after 4...Bb4+, and what is the plan?

cards.back: 5.Nc3 4...Bb4+ is best answered by developing with Nc3 and Bd3, preparing kingside castling.

front.text: Which 2 moves do we develop with after 4...Nf6, and what do they prepare?

cards.back: We develop with [5.Nc3] and [5.Bd3], preparing kingside castling.

front.text: How good is our position after 3...cxd4?! 4.cxd4 d5 5.e5! ?

cards.back:
This line offers White good chances. Black has transposed to a worse version of the French, and we have a nice advantage and good attacking chances.

A good illustration of the key ideas is the game M. Socko − P. Ofstad.

front.text: What is your move after 3...d5, and why not 4.e5 ?

cards.back:
4.exd5 This move aligns with our repertoire choice against the French Defense.

After [4.e5], we would transpose to the main line of the French Advance Variation 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3, which is not part of our repertoire. I considered this line but felt that Black usually feels more at home in these structures when they opt for the French.

3...d5 looks like Black's best option.

front.text: What are Black's 2 main moves after 4.exd5, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [4...exd5] Black takes with the pawn and avoids the transposition after the queen move.
- [4...Qxd5] would again lead to a transposition. This position is covered via [2...d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.d4 e6], which is a more common way to get to the same situation.

front.text: After 4...exd5, which French line is this with colors reversed, and what is our plan?

cards.back:
With White, we play 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 exd5 4.c4 against the French, when 4...Nf6 5.Nc3 c6 is a common continuation. Here, in the Sicilian, we switch sides but enjoy an extra tempo! This extra tempo is important because the position is wide open.

We want to make use of it by developing quickly. The best way to do it is playing our knight to f3 and our bishop to b5, trying to castle as fast as possible.

front.text: What is your move after 4...exd5, and how does it compare with 5.Nf3 ?

cards.back: 5.Bb5+ I like this a bit more than [5.Nf3], but both moves will likely lead to the same positions − we want to play both anyway.

front.text: What are Black's 2 main moves after 5.Bb5+, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [5...Nc6] claude: Black blocks the check with a developing move.
- [5...Bd7] Then [5...Bd7 | 6.Bxd7+ Nxd7 7.Nf3] followed by O-O. We develop quickly and will be the first to operate on the e-file.

front.text: What is your move after 5...Nc6 and why?

cards.back:
6.Nf3 No surprises, but good moves. We want to castle next and get our rook into the game. Black's king is still on e8, and the e-file is wide open!

This position is only slightly better for White if Black plays perfectly. In practice, this proves difficult.

front.text: What are Black's 2 main moves after 6.Nf3, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [6...Bd6]! is best, but it is not an obvious move. The idea is that Black can block a check on the e-file with the move ...Nge7.
- [6...Nf6] is less reliable for Black. [6...Nf6 | 7.O-O Be7 8.dxc5 Bxc5 9.Bg5] shows a drawback of ...Nf6: the pin is annoying for Black.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 6...Bd6! ?

cards.back:
- 7.dxc5 claude: Black's d-pawn is left isolated.
- 7...Bxc5 claude: Black takes back.
- 8.O-O We want to castle and get our rook into the game.

front.text: After 8...Nge7, how do we stand and what is our plan?

cards.back:
After 8...Nge7, Black's king is safe for the moment. Black's knight on e7 is not ideally placed, but the king's safety is more important.

We have a small advantage in this position, trying to exploit the isolated d-pawn. The next step is Nb1-d2-b3, increasing our control of the d4-square. We want to trade as many minor pieces as possible, as each trade makes the isolated pawn more vulnerable in an endgame.

front.text: What are the next 5 plies following 6...Nf6 ?

cards.back:
- 7.O-O We want to castle and get our rook into the game.
- 7...Be7 claude: Black gets ready to castle.
- 8.dxc5 claude: Black's d-pawn is left isolated.
- 8...Bxc5 claude: Black takes back.
- 9.Bg5 shows a drawback of ...Nf6: the pin is annoying for Black.

We'll follow a similar strategy as against [6...Bd6] (Nb1-d2-b3 next) and have good chances for an advantage.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 5...Bd7 ?

cards.back:
- 6.Bxd7+ claude: We trade bishops and keep developing.
- 6...Nxd7 claude: Black takes back with the knight.
- 7.Nf3 followed by O-O. We develop quickly and will be the first to operate on the e-file.

front.text: What is the conclusion on 2...e6 ?

cards.back:
If they continue with optimal play, 2...e6 is a reasonable choice for Black. In practice, however, Black often invites a transposition to a worse version of the French, which we happily accept. We have a nice advantage and good attacking chances after [3.d4 cxd4 | 4.cxd4 d5 5.e5]!

A better option for Black is 3...d5, which leads to a different pawn structure after [3.d4 d5 | 4.exd5 exd5], and usually features an IQP on our opponent's side. We can castle quickly and are quicker on the e-file, which makes it easier for us to play.

front.text: What is Black's idea with 2...d5 against the Alapin?

cards.back:
On the master level, Black usually chooses between two replies to the Alapin: [2...Nf6] and 2...d5. Both moves share a common concept: Black attacks our e-pawn immediately and forces our pawn to capture or advance.

We don't get the opportunity to realize our main strategic goal, which is to establish a perfect pawn duo in the center. Lines like [2...d6 3.d4] or [2...e6 3.d4] allow us to build the desired pawn formation.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 2...d5 ?

cards.back:
- 3.exd5 Taking the pawn is best. We open the position and have good chances to gain a bit of time on Black's queen after their recapture.
- 3...Qxd5 Moving the queen early in the opening is often a dubious idea. In this concrete case, Black's play is justified if they continue in the correct way.
- 4.d4 Our natural reply. Now we need to consider three basic scenarios.

front.text: After 3...Qxd5, why can't we gain time with Nc3 as in the Scandinavian, and what should Black avoid?

cards.back:
Moving the queen early in the opening is often a dubious idea. The queen, being the most valuable piece, can get chased around by lesser pieces. In this concrete case, Black's play is justified if they continue in the correct way.

The key point to understand is that as long as our pawn is on c3, the queen can't be attacked by the move Nc3. This is a key difference to the Scandinavian 1.e4 [1...d5 2.exd5 Qxd5 3.Nc3], when 3.Nc3 develops the knight with a tempo gain. In our Alapin line, Black should avoid this scenario.

That is why [4.d4 | 4...cxd4]?! is a conceptual mistake: after [4.d4 cxd4 | 5.cxd4], we are ready to play Nc3 with a gain of time.

front.text: What are Black's 4 main moves after 4.d4, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [4...cxd4]?! is very popular below master-level, but a conceptual mistake. After [4...cxd4 | 5.cxd4], we are ready to play Nc3 with a gain of time.
- [4...Nf6] Black correctly avoids the trade. [4...Nf6 | 5.Nf3 Bg4] aims for an active development of the c8-bishop, [4...Nf6 5.Nf3 | 5...e6] for quick kingside development.
- [4...Nc6] Black correctly avoids the trade and aims for a setup with an active development of the c8-bishop, for example, after [4...Nc6 | 5.Nf3 Bg4].
- [4...e6] Black avoids the trade and aims for quick kingside development, keeping the bishop on c8 for a while.

front.text: What is your move after 4...Nf6, and where can it lead?

cards.back:
5.Nf3 We play the natural moves Nf3, Be2 and O-O in all cases.

After [5...Bg4 6.Be2], the position is similar to the 4...Nc6 line. After [5...e6], Black aims for quick kingside development, as in the 4...e6 line. It's all easy for us to handle, as we'll play Nf3, Be2, and O-O anyway.

front.text: What is your move after 4...cxd4?! and why are we happy to see it?

cards.back: 5.cxd4 We are happy to see 4...cxd4?!, as now we are ready to attack Black's queen with Nc3, gaining a valuable tempo for our development.

front.text: What are Black's 2 main moves after 5.cxd4, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [5...Nc6] Black attacks our d-pawn, a very logical and popular move.
- [5...Nf6] You'll also meet this. [5...Nf6 | 6.Nc3] develops with tempo, and after the most popular queen move, [5...Nf6 6.Nc3 | 6...Qd8 7.Bc4] gives us some advantage.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 5...Nf6, and which Caro-Kann line reaches the same position?

cards.back:
- 6.Nc3 Developing with tempo.
- 6...Qd8 Black has a choice of various queen moves. Most popular is 6...Qd8.
- 7.Bc4 A normal development move like 7.Bc4 gives us some advantage.

It is interesting to compare this position to the Caro-Kann, as 1.e4 [1...c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 Nf6 5.Nc3 dxc4 6.Bxc4] may lead to the same position. It pays off to follow similar concepts across different openings, as you reach familiar structures.

front.text: What is your move after 5...Nc6, and why not 6.Nc3 ?

cards.back:
6.Nf3 We need to cover our pawn.

[6.Nc3]? [6.Nc3 | 6...Qxd4] drops our most important pawn.

5...Nc6 attacks our d-pawn, a very logical and popular move.

front.text: What are Black's 3 main moves after 6.Nf3, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [6...Bg4] The most active and most popular move for Black.
- [6...Nf6]? [6...Nf6 | 7.Nc3 Qd8 8.d5] leads to a disaster, as Black needs to return their knight to b8.
- [6...e6] is a better move, but [6...e6 | 7.Nc3] is still nice for White. Black should delay or omit the trade on d4.

front.text: After 6...Nf6?, what are the next 3 plies, and why is it a disaster for Black?

cards.back:
- 7.Nc3 claude: The knight hits the queen with tempo.
- 7...Qd8 claude: The queen retreats.
- 8.d5 leads to a disaster, as Black needs to return their knight to b8. We gain too much time and get an attack for free.

front.text: What is your move after 6...e6, and what should Black have done instead?

cards.back:
7.Nc3 is still nice for White. claude: The knight develops with tempo on the queen.

6...e6 is a better move than [6...Nf6], but we discuss a similar setup via [4...e6], which is more precise. Black should delay or omit the trade on d4.

front.text: What is your move after 6...Bg4, and why not 7.Nc3 ?

cards.back:
7.Be2 We need to break the pin first. After [7.Nc3 Bxf3]! the game gets very sharp and hard to assess.

We should play 7.Be2, also for an additional reason. Black may play [4...Nc6 5.Nf3 Bg4 6.Be2 cxd4 7.cxd4], which leads to the same position.

6...Bg4 is the most active and most popular move for Black.

front.text: What are Black's 2 main moves after 7.Be2, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [7...Bxf3]? A bad move, but the worst is yet to come... After [7...Bxf3 | 8.Bxf3], we have a large advantage in any case.

front.text: What is the conclusion on 2...d5 ?

cards.back:
2...d5 is one of the best replies to the Alapin, but Black needs to know more than that. After the trade on d4, we gain some time on Black's queen, and they need to play precisely because they are slightly behind in development. Our play is fairly easy. We have a standard way to develop, based on Nf3, Be2, and a quick O-O.

After [3.exd5 Qxd5 4.d4], Black will usually trade on d4 at some point, often immediately on the fourth move. The resulting pawn structure, the IQP (Isolated Queen's Pawn) is a common guest in our repertoire. In exchange for a potential weakness of the d-pawn, we can develop our pieces to active squares and often grab the initiative. In most cases, we'll win a tempo on Black's queen by playing Nc3.

front.text: What is the upside of 4...e6, and which other move orders lead to this setup?

cards.back:
Black locks in their c8-bishop, which looks a bit passive. Their setup has an upside, though: Black emphasizes kingside development and usually manages to castle quickly.

Black can also start with a knight move and then play the pawn to e6. For example, [4...Nf6 5.Nf3 e6] or [4...Nc6 5.Nf3 Nf6 6.Be2 e6] are common sequences. It's all easy for us to handle, as we'll play Nf3, Be2, and O-O anyway.

front.text: What are the next 5 plies following 4...e6, and why do we prefer 6.Be2 to other bishop moves?

cards.back:
- 5.Nf3 We get closer to castling by playing Nf3 and Be2 next.
- 5...Nf6 claude: Black develops the kingside knight.
- 6.Be2 I recommend sticking with this bishop development. We usually place the bishop on e2 in this chapter, often as a more or less forced reply to ...Bg4. In the current position, there is no pin on our knight, which gives us more options. It is perfectly possible to go for [6.Bd3], [6.Be3], or the interesting [6.Na3] (intending Nb5), but having a universal setup based on Be2 cuts down our memory load immensely.
- 6...Nc6 The most natural development scheme for Black is ...Nc6, ...Be7, then castling. It doesn't matter if they start with the knight or bishop move.
- 7.O-O Our king is safe now.

front.text: After 7.O-O, why would we be happy to see ...cxd4 ?

cards.back: Black has avoided the trade of c-pawns so far. They could have inserted ...cxd4 at any given moment, but we'd be happy about it. As discussed before, the trade gives us the option Nc3, gaining an important tempo for our development.

Black's main idea behind 2...Nf6 is to lure our pawns forward and then attack them. Black will often play moves like ...Nc6 or ...d6, soon attacking our advanced pawn.

front.text: After 3...Nd5, what is our plan?

cards.back: Our idea is simple: we want to play our d-pawn to d4 and develop the kingside by playing Nf3, Bc4 and finally, castle. This logical concept works well against various setups that Black may try.

front.text: What is the conclusion on 2...Nf6 ?

cards.back:
2...Nf6 is a main line on the master level for a good reason. The resulting positions are interesting to play for both sides and give Black good chances to equalize the game.

Our approach against it is quite simple. We play the natural moves d4, Nf3, and Bc4, getting ready for kingside castling. We have established a pawn on e5, which gives us an advantage in space, while Black has a strong square for their knight. Black has a range of options on how to place their central pawns, but our play is quite similar in all cases and follows basic opening principles.

front.text: What is your move after 6...d6, and why not 7.Bd3 ?

cards.back:
7.Bc4 The best development option for our bishop.

The move [7.Bd3] is less precise because Black has [7.Bd3 | 7...dxe5 8.dxe5 Nb4], when we need to move the bishop again and allow a queen trade. These trades only help Black, as they have less space.

6...d6 This is Black's most popular choice, attacking the e5-pawn. This position may also arise via [5...d6 6.cxd4 e6], of course. Black has alternatives to 6...d6, but they don't change our plans: we develop our bishop to c4 and castle kingside.

front.text: After 7.Bc4, what is our plan, and why avoid trades?

cards.back:
We should keep more pieces on the board, as the advanced e-pawn might help us to generate an attack on the kingside. Black's knight is nicely placed on d5, but it no longer defends the kingside.

After castling kingside first, a common idea for White is to activate the queen via Qd1-e2-e4 to the kingside.
